modules.title: Our team and values
modules.body_md:
## Who we are

Window Works has been taking care of homes in the Triangle since 2007. We're
family owned, and the expertise behind us goes back a lot further than the
company does.

Our founder, Jeff, has been selling windows and doors since the early 1970s. His
son Justin remembers climbing over window boxes as a toddler, and as soon as he
was old enough he began delivering, installing, and selling them. That history is
worth knowing because customers ask about it.

The company runs in five functions.

**Leadership** is Jeff as CEO, Justin as COO, and Rose as CTO. They set
direction and own the decisions that cross departments.

**Project management** hires and oversees the installation subcontractors, and
is the main contact for homeowners once a job moves into install.

**Admin** handles payroll, scheduling, and the paperwork behind every job.

**Marketing** runs the blog, the website, social media, and our reviews and
reputation. Everything a customer sees before they ever call us.

**Sales** splits into B2B and B2C. B2B works with contractors, custom home
builders, and DIYers. B2C is homeowners and in-home sales, and we usually
install. People work one side or the other, not both.

## Who to go to

You'll hit things the training doesn't cover, and the answer is usually one of
five people. This is the whole list.

**Technology Officer (Rose)**

- Anything involving a Free in-home sales consultation activity: moving it,
  renaming it, rescheduling it (Effective activity management)
- Marketing material you've made yourself, before you use it (Generating your own
  leads)
- Funding for an event you want to run (Generating your own leads)
- Anything to do with CompanyCam (Taking great pictures in CompanyCam)
- Any question about the tech we use, and anything in the portal, Pipedrive, or
  Vendo that looks broken

**Project manager (Keith)**

- Anything about how a job will actually be installed
- Site conditions you're unsure about

**COO (Justin)**

- A competing quote that looks genuinely equivalent to ours (The Value Match
  Guarantee)
- Whether we take a job on at all, where the construction is unusual enough to
  be a concern (Winning and losing a deal)
- Specialty windows, meaning an odd shape or a size the standard lines won't
  build (400 Series specialty windows)
- Moving glass walls and big doors, once you've set the expectation (The lineup,
  and Quoting big doors)

**Justin and Rose**

- Any discount over 20 percent, which Vendo routes automatically (How our pricing
  works, and Using Vendo)

**Admin (Brandon)**

- Payments, deposits, and anything that has to be recorded against a deal
  (Winning and losing a deal)
- Your commission calculator each pay period (Your commission calculator)
- Scheduling, including the final measure (Essential customer information)

## When you don't know who

Ask anyone. Good judgment is valued here, and so is not sitting on something for
a day because you weren't sure who owned it.

## Our core values

There are seven, and every person in the company is measured against the same
seven.

- Honest and reliable
- Problem solving
- Good customer service
- Strong sales
- Strong work ethic
- Technical competence
- Engaged

**Some of them won't look like your job, and that's deliberate.** Good customer
service is on the scorecard for an installer. Strong sales is on it for admin.
We think everyone here is accountable for things that aren't in their job title.

These are what your evaluation scores. The employment contract module covers how
that works.

## Things we believe at Window Works

**Customer service is everyone's job.** Not sales, not the installer, not the
PM. Every person is empowered to make sure the customer has a good experience.

**Each of us is a guide.** We exist to help customers find windows and doors
they'll love. If the customer is the hero of their own story, we're the guide.
The Yoda to their Luke Skywalker, the Cher Horowitz to their Tai Frasier.
Whatever your role, your primary task is creating conversations and tools that
educate them so they make the right choice.

**Good judgment is valued and usually rewarded.** If a decision needs making
and nobody is around, use your best judgment.

**Fast is better than slow** unless there's a compelling reason to go slow.
That doesn't mean rushing into mistakes.

**Our time and energy are our most valuable assets.** This is why we hold
product minimums, service area limits, and other boundaries so firmly. We'll
cover what all of those are in later modules.

**We're growing,** which means stretching and changing. Something set up one
way may change in six or twelve months, and we want to be clear about that from
day one.

**Always be thinking about streamlining.** If you find a way to save time and
effort that also improves the customer experience, tell us. There's a good
chance it becomes how we do it.

**Never guarantee something you can't personally deliver.** If a customer asks
for a specific salesperson and they're out, don't promise they'll call back
today. Say you'll tell them they called as soon as they're back. This builds
trust. Promising what you can't deliver breaks it.

**We don't do silos.** Teams share openly across functions. Marketing gets
photos of installations in progress and after they're finished, but they rely
on sales for good before shots taken at the initial consultation. You'll get
guidance on exactly what they need during training on CompanyCam, the app we use
to photograph every job.

**Do it, then report it.** Rather than saying you'll work on something, get it
done and say it's done. Always close the communication loop.

**Keep information where other people can find it.** Subscriptions go to the
company address, not your personal one. We never use personal email for company
business.

**Own your mistakes.** Examine them, learn, tell people as soon as you notice,
then move on. Did you have a bad day, or a few bad minutes in an otherwise fine
day? The difference matters.

**More knowledge makes us more successful.** Every role here goes deep on
technical detail, whether tech stack or product. It's more than anyone can hand
you directly, so read, ask, watch, and go find what you need.

modules.title: Employment contract and company policies
modules.body_md:
## Your contract

It covers:

- The benefits you're entitled to
- Your first 90 days, with a review at the end
- Our right to drug and alcohol testing
- Maintenance and return of company property
- Paid time off, which starts after that 90 day review

Both sides sign and you keep a copy.

## Your 90 day review

This is your first evaluation, and after it they're annual.

You fill in a scorecard on yourself. Justin and Rose fill in the same scorecard
on you. It covers the seven core values, and each one is marked as consistent,
sometimes, or not usually.

The forms don't get swapped. You sit down and talk through what each of you put,
and the places where your score and theirs don't match are usually where the
useful conversation is.

If something needs discussing before 90 days, it will be. You won't be sitting on
a surprise until November.

## Conduct

This is a non-discriminatory workplace. Harassment or discrimination against coworkers,
customers, or anyone else based on protected characteristics is prohibited.
Report anything immediately to your supervisor, or above them if they are
involved. We investigate promptly and confidentially.

Divisive topics can be discussed respectfully. They can't be discussed in a way
that disrupts work or creates a hostile environment.

Tell your supervisor about any accommodation you need.

Working under the influence of drugs or alcohol is grounds for termination.
That covers driving, jobsites, customer homes, and the showroom. Occasions where
the company provides alcohol are company events, and they're announced as
such.

## Your week

Full time is 40 hours.

- **Appointments** run between 10 and 6:30, Monday to Friday
- **Weekends** are never scheduled for you. If a customer warrants it you can
  choose to meet them then
- **Showroom** is eight hours a week, on a schedule we'll set with you and
  review at the end of your training
- **Department meeting** is one hour a week
- **Follow up** counts. Chasing quotes, answering questions, and staying in
  front of people who haven't decided is the work, not something extra you fit
  around it

The store itself runs Monday to Friday, 8:30 to 5.

## If you're out

Call or text your supervisor no later than 30 minutes before your start time,
and check in each day you're out unexpectedly. You can skip the daily check in
once your supervisor knows the situation and roughly how long you'll be gone.

Three consecutive no call no show days is treated as voluntary job abandonment
and ends employment.

## Equipment and appearance

You maintain the equipment assigned to you. Negligence or loss may be your
financial responsibility. Normal wear and tear is not.

Dress code applies to all customer-facing and office roles: sales, admin,
operations, and project management.

- Clean and wrinkle-free, no holes or stains
- Company or vendor branded tops are fine, and any logo stays smaller than a
  credit card
- No hoods unless they're Window Works branded, and hats only if they're
  Window Works or vendor branded
- Khaki, navy, black, or gray bottoms. Clean jeans are fine. No cargo, no
  corduroy, no stretch or knit pants
- Closed toe professional shoes
- Hair in a natural color
- No offensive language or imagery on clothing
- Jewelry that won't catch on product you're handling
- Name tag at a customer's house, and when you're on assigned showroom
  coverage. Not needed otherwise in the office

When you're doing manual work in the course of the job, unloading windows or
anything like it, your safety and comfort come first. Dress for that.

For anyone based in the office: everyone keeps their own space clean and
we collectively handle shared areas and trash. Cleaners come weekly or
biweekly, we cover the gaps.

## Technology and confidentiality

Company technology is for business use.

Don't disclose proprietary, financial, customer, or operational information
outside the company. What you see in a customer's home stays there.

On personal social media you speak for yourself, but confidentiality and
anti-harassment still apply.

## Internal communication

**Pipedrive, our CRM, is the primary channel** for anything about a specific
customer or job. Every deal lives there, and so does the conversation about it.
Email is next, where Pipedrive doesn't fit.

**All business through your company email.**

**Respond to email within four business hours.** If it's informational,
acknowledge it. If it asks for a short action, do it and say it's done. Don't
reply saying you'll work on it. If it's a longer task, give your best
estimate and email again when it's finished.

Out for a full day or more: set an out of office naming your backup.

## Personal vehicle and mileage

You use your own vehicle and we reimburse the miles at the federal standard
rate. Your personal insurance is primary.

MileIQ is required, and the module on it covers what counts and what doesn't.

## PTO

We're paid biweekly. Pay periods, pay dates, the holiday calendar, and your
current sick and vacation balances are all in the Window Works Team Portal.

**Five sick days and ten vacation days a year, plus eleven paid holidays.**

### How you get them

Nothing accrues during your first 90 days. After your 90 day review you start
earning a portion of each per full month worked, so your first year builds up
rather than arriving whole. The exact rate is 0.4167 sick days and 0.8333
vacation days per full month.

From the next January 1 onward, the full five and ten land at once at the start
of the year.

### Requesting it

Requests go in the Window Works Team Portal.

**It isn't approved until the request shows as approved.** If you haven't heard
back, follow up.

Vacation goes in at least 30 days ahead, in writing. Changes need a new request
and new approval.

### Sick leave

Covers you, or a family member who needs care. Child, partner, parent, and so
on. For more than one consecutive day, your approver may ask for a note from a
healthcare provider.

### What happens to unused days

No rollover. Up to five unused vacation days are paid out annually. Everything
is forfeited on resignation or termination.

modules.title: Who you're selling to
modules.body_md:
Most of the people you sit down with have never bought windows before, and most
of them never will again. That single fact shapes almost everything about the
appointment.

They have no reference point. They don't know what a window costs, what a good
installation looks like, or what questions to ask. They aren't being difficult
when they can't tell you what they want. They genuinely don't know yet.

## The number in their head is wrong

**This is the one that catches people out.** Homeowners routinely arrive
expecting a figure that's off by a factor of ten or more.

It isn't their fault. They've seen advertising for windows at a few hundred
dollars installed, or buy one get one free, and that's the anchor they walked in
with. Nobody advertises what a properly installed window actually costs, so the
cheapest possible number is the only one in circulation.

Our average project is $22,745. If somebody was expecting two or three thousand
for the whole house, the gap isn't a negotiation. It's an education, and it
happens before any conversation about our price can land.

Which is why the pricing conversation comes early rather than at the end. A
number that arrives after ninety minutes of building rapport feels like a
reveal. The same number early on is just information.

## What they're actually worried about

Very little of it is the window.

They're worried about being ripped off, about being pressured into signing, about
the mess, and about a contractor who does a bad job and disappears. A lot of them
have had a bad experience with somebody in the trades before, and they're
carrying it into your appointment.

Our own guide to buying windows puts it plainly: loving your windows means not
feeling confused, overwhelmed, pressured, or ripped off at any point in the
process.

That's the standard, and it's a useful one to measure an appointment against.

modules.title: Our installation standards
modules.body_md:
The best window in the world fails if it's installed badly. Anyone can sell the
same window. Almost nobody installs it the way we do.

You'll lose deals on price. You shouldn't lose them on price without the
customer understanding what they're giving up.

## The problem with our differentiator

Everything that separates our installation from a cheap one is **invisible once
the job is done.** Two windows can look the same the day they go in. The
installation is what decides how they look and work ten or twenty years from
now. One will still be sealed. The other will be letting air and water into the
wall.

That's exactly why the cheap version skimps on these things. Nobody sees them.

Which means the invisible parts have to come up during the appointment, before
the numbers get compared.

## The three things we do differently

### 1. No capping, we replace the trim

Capping means wrapping aluminum coil over the existing exterior wood trim
rather than replacing it.

It's fast, it's cheap, and it looks fine on day one. It also traps whatever was
underneath. If there's rot, capping hides it and lets it keep going, out of
sight, into the wall of the house.

We replace the trim. PVC on the outside, which won't rot.

When a customer has a quote that includes capping, that isn't a cheaper version
of our job. It's a different job.

**A real world example.** A homeowner with an Andersen E-Series window
(Andersen's top of the line, aluminum clad over wood) called us because it was
leaking. They
assumed the window was bad. We ran a water test, spraying at specific points on
and around the unit to isolate where the water was getting in.

The window was fine. Rot around the opening had never been repaired when the
previous window was replaced. Once the rot was fixed, the leak stopped.

The best window available failed because of what somebody skipped years
earlier. Rot that gets covered instead of cut out doesn't go away, and
eventually the customer blames the window.

### 2. Correct sealing

**Minimal-expansion polyurethane foam formulated for windows and doors,**
around the full perimeter. Standard expanding foam from a hardware store bows
the frame. It isn't the same product and it does real damage.

**Silicone-based caulk.** The exterior caulk sold at big box stores is acrylic.
It's cheap and readily available, and it doesn't flex enough. It gets brittle,
cracks, and then you have gaps, water, and rot. Silicone stays elastic and moves
with the window for years.

**Properly tooled, on a surface that was cleaned first.** A good caulk job
isn't noticeable. A bad one has globs in some places and thin, tearing beads in
others, and that inconsistency is where the water gets in.

> **Tooling** is pressing the bead into the joint after it's run, so it grips
> both sides instead of sitting on top of the gap.

### 3. A correct expansion joint

An expansion joint is the space left around the window during installation, the
gap between the window frame and the home's siding. Both materials need room to
move.

**We recommend 5/16 inch on most projects.** Materials may shift it, but 5/16
is typical.

This matters more here than most places. Central North Carolina can swing 70
degrees in a few days, and with our humidity, everything moves: the brick or
siding, the window frame, the casing and moulding, and the caulk itself.

**Many contractors consistently leave the gap too small or too large, and both
lead to failure.** Too small and the frame bows when it tries to expand with
nowhere to go, which is where sticking sashes and failed seals come from. Too
large and the caulk breaks down, because it's filling more space than it can
function across.

## Plumb, level, and square

Before any of the above, the window has to sit right in the opening.

- **Plumb.** The sides are perpendicular to a level sill.
- **Level.** Across both the sill and the head.
- **Square.** Every corner is 90 degrees and the unit isn't racked.

Nearly every operational problem in a window traces back to one of those three.

## The rest of our install standards

- Flashing integration appropriate to the installation type, the materials
  used, and the products themselves
- Interior and exterior trim on full frame installations
- Debris haul away and dumping

## The seven signs of a bad installation, and how to use them

This is the most useful thing you can do in the first ten minutes of an
appointment. Look at the windows they already have and tell them what you see.

1. **A window that won't open.** The sash can't glide because the unit isn't plumb, level, or square.
2. **A window that won't lock.** Lock and keeper are out of alignment. Same
   root cause.
3. **Rain, wind, dust, or bugs coming through a closed window.** An indicator
   the window isn't airtight.
4. **Sashes that won't stay put.** Raise it and it creeps or drops.
5. **A sill that isn't level.** Raise the sash slightly, or crank the casement
   partway, and look at the gap between sash and sill. That gap is called the
   reveal. It should be even across the whole span. If it's not, the unit is
   bowed, crowned, or angled.
6. **Poor caulking.** Globs and thin spots, or the wrong caulk entirely.
7. **No proper expansion joint,** or one that's far too large.

## The door version: the reveal

Just as plumb, level, and square tell you how well a window was installed, the
reveal tells you how well a door was. With one caveat that matters here more
than it does most places.

{{video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i-26FxEO0D8}}

The door reveal is the gap between the door panel and the frame around it. On a
good install it's even the whole way around. Never perfect, but close.

Follow the gap from top to bottom. Tight or touching at the top and wider
toward the bottom means the reveal is off. Visible rubbing is the same signal.

An uneven reveal means the door will stick, rub, or fight you when it seals.
The homeowner may not have noticed yet, but over time the issue will become
more and more noticeable.

**Be honest about the cause.** An uneven reveal isn't automatically a bad
install. The other cause is the house moving, and around here that's common.
The Triangle sits on heavy clay, and homes here never really stop shifting. A door installed correctly forty years ago can be out of reveal
today through no fault of anyone.

Saying that out loud is more credible than blaming whoever came before you, and
it sets up the sale rather than undercutting it.

**And there are products designed to live with settling.** Andersen 400 Series
hinged patio doors have adjustable hinges that let you raise, lower, or shift
the panel. Their gliding doors adjust with a Phillips head at the roller. So
when you tell a homeowner their door is out of reveal because the house moved,
you can follow it immediately with a door that can be brought back into
alignment when it happens again. That's a real reason to choose a better door,
and it's specific to this market.

## The warranty

**Window Works offers a two year warranty on workmanship for products we
install, beginning from the date of installation.**

Manufacturer defects, including glass seal
failure and hardware failure, run through the manufacturer's warranty. Voided
by negligence, acts of God, or modifications by anyone other than us, including
the homeowner.

It's one of the four things the Value Match Guarantee compares against, and a
competitor offering one year doesn't qualify as equivalent.

## Who actually does the work

Vetted subcontractor crews, managed directly by our project manager, who hires
them, oversees them, walks the jobs, and is the direct contact for much of the
installation work.

**Our lead crew has been with us since we founded the company, in 2007.** That
isn't a small thing in this trade, and it's worth saying out loud. Crews that
stay are crews that are treated well and paid properly, and that shows up in
the work.

## How to use this at the table

Bring it up before the price conversation, not after. Once someone is comparing
two numbers it's too late to explain why they aren't comparable.

**The deck does most of this for you.** The installation section in Ingage opens
with Justin explaining how we install, then a slide with a popup on each of the
three: no capping, correct sealing, and a correct expansion joint. Walk them
through those rather than describing them from memory.

Use the words anyway. Most homeowners have never heard anyone talk about
installation at this level and it lands.

If they have another quote, ask what it says about the sealing and the expansion
joint and whether they're capping. It usually doesn't say, and the question is more
persuasive than any claim you could make.

If they genuinely want the cheaper build, offer to re-spec our quote down to
that scope so the choice is theirs and fully informed. Most decline once they
see it written out.

## Related reading

Here are some articles from our blog that may be helpful to homeowners as they
research window and door replacement options.

- [Seven Telltale Signs of a Bad Window Installation](https://www.windowworksnc.com/seven-telltale-signs-of-a-bad-window-installation/)
- [A Simple Water Test Can Determine if Windows Were Improperly Installed](https://www.windowworksnc.com/a-simple-water-test-can-determine-if-the-windows-in-your-home-were-improperly-installed/)
- [What Is a Door Reveal? How to Tell If Your Door Was Installed Right](https://www.windowworksnc.com/what-is-a-door-reveal-how-to-tell-if-your-door-was-installed-right/)
- [Should You Cap Your Windows? What Homeowners Need to Know](https://www.windowworksnc.com/should-you-cap-your-windows-what-homeowners-need-to-know/)
- [Are Windows Installed from the Inside or the Outside of a Home?](https://www.windowworksnc.com/are-windows-installed-from-the-inside-or-the-outside-of-a-home/)

quiz.q: What's wrong with standard expanding foam around a window?
options: It cures too slowly to shim against the same day
It breaks down under UV and has to be covered by trim
It bows the frame, so we use minimal-expansion polyurethane
It can't be used below forty degrees, which limits winter work

quiz.q: What expansion joint do we recommend on most projects?
options: 2/16 inch
4/16 inch
8/16 inch
5/16 inch

quiz.q: You're in a home looking at windows another company installed three years ago. The caulk is cracked and pulling away, and the gaps between frame and siding are wide. What most likely went wrong at install?
options: The joint was too tight and the frame has been squeezed
Acrylic caulk was used instead of silicone
The joint was left too wide for the caulk to span
The siding was never back-primed before it went on

quiz.q: Why do we use silicone caulk rather than the acrylic sold at big box stores?
options: It costs less per tube on a job this size
It can be painted over, where acrylic can't
It cures faster in cold weather, so we can shim the same day
It stays elastic where acrylic goes brittle and cracks

quiz.q: A customer's front door is tight at the top corner and the gap widens toward the bottom. What do you tell them?
options: The reveal is off, from the install or the house moving
The slab has dropped and the threshold needs shimming
The weatherstrip has compressed unevenly over time
The hinges have sagged and need to be shimmed out

quiz.q: Why is our installation quality a hard thing to sell?
options: What separates it from a cheap install is hidden once finished
Competitors make the same claims about their own crews
Customers rarely meet the installing crew before they sign
It adds cost that does not show in the product itself

modules.title: MileIQ and expense submission
modules.body_md:
You drive a lot in this role. This is how you get paid for it.

## The rate

The federal standard mileage rate.
[Look up the current rate](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/standard-mileage-rates). It covers fuel, insurance,
maintenance, and depreciation. There's no separate gas reimbursement, because
the rate already includes it.

## The monthly cutoff

Classify each trip as business or personal in the MileIQ app. The cutoff for
any given month is **the first of the following month**.

## What counts

**Your first trip of the day isn't reimbursed**, wherever it's going. Whether
that's a customer's house or the showroom, it's your commute.

**Everything after it is.** Once you're out, moving between locations is
reimbursable. A location can be somewhere assigned, like a customer's home or
the showroom, or a temporary workspace like a coffee shop or library where
you're working from.

Personal errands and detours aren't reimbursable.

## Parking and tolls

Reimbursable between appointments, logged as incidental expenses with receipts
attached.

## If you get stuck

The app is straightforward, but MileIQ has a
[playlist of short how-to videos](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLq8MD0g8eAn9NIvmS1b87S_689N9DVp0y)
if you want one.

home-to-appointment to be reimbursed tax free, on the basis that the showroom is
a regular work location. We're choosing not to. Since 2017 a W-2 employee can't
deduct the difference themselves, so the rep absorbs it. Exposure only runs the
other way: paying for a commute tax free would be the payroll problem, and we
don't.

NCDOL treats mileage as a promised wage benefit, so whatever this module says is
what the company is bound to. Change it carefully.

modules.title: How you get paid
modules.body_md:
## The structure

**Base salary: $20,000 per year.**

**Your first four weeks are paid at the equivalent of $40,000 annually.**
Training pay, so you aren't trying to learn the job and produce at the same
time. It ends when you go live in the field.

## Commission

| | Up to $2M | Over $2M |
|---|---|---|
| Company generated leads | 8% | 10% |
| Rep generated leads | 10% | 13% |

The $2M is your total annual volume, not a figure per lead type.

## What else you get

**Mileage** at the federal standard rate, tracked in MileIQ.

## When you get paid

**Commission is paid as the money comes in.** When the deposit is collected you
are paid on that share of the sale. When the final payment is collected you are
paid on the rest.

The deposit is collected at the Measurement Confirmation appointment, so a deal
you close in your first week can be earning that same week.

**Financed jobs pay you on the same schedule.** The customer puts nothing down
and Synchrony doesn't pay us until the job is complete, but your commission
still follows the deposit and the final payment the way it would on a cash job.

So sell whichever way suits the customer. It makes no difference to when you get
paid.

modules.title: Your commission calculator
modules.body_md:
Commission is tracked by hand right now. Automated tracking arrives with the new
CRM, and until then the calculator is the record of what you're owed.

It's a spreadsheet, and you're issued your own.

## Commission follows the payment, not the deal

A deal doesn't pay you all at once. **The deposit earns commission when the
deposit is collected, and the balance earns commission when the balance is
collected.**

So a job you close in August with a deposit collected that week earns you
commission that week. The rest arrives when the customer pays the rest, which is
usually after installation.

On a staged job, where the work splits across more than one visit, each invoice
is a payment and earns commission when it lands.

## The customer payments are already in the CRM

To be clear about which payments these are: this is money customers pay us, not
commission we pay you. Every time a customer pays, admin logs it against the
deal in a collect payment activity, with the method, the last four or the check
number, and the amount.

You don't record those. Your job is to read them across. Go through your won
deals, find the customer payments logged since you last did this, and add a line
to the calculator for each one.

## Filling in a line

Four columns you fill, two that fill themselves.

- **Date.** When the customer paid
- **PO #.** So it can be matched back to the job. The
  [PO naming](module:REF-080) sheet has the convention
- **Lead Generated By.** A dropdown, either Window Works or Employee. This is
  what sets your rate, so it's the one to get right
- **Payment received (PRE TAX).** The amount the customer paid with the sales
  tax taken out. Tax isn't yours and isn't ours, so it isn't in the commission
- **Comission Earned** calculates itself from the rate and the amount
- **Notes** if anything about the line needs explaining

The total at the top adds up every line, and that total is what you're owed for
the period.

## Email it to admin each pay period

Pay periods are biweekly and the calendar is on the Resources tab in the portal.

**Admin needs your calculator by end of day Tuesday.** Payroll runs Wednesday
and paychecks go out Friday, so Tuesday is the cutoff for anything to land that
week.

The calculator is what payroll works from, so a payment that isn't on it won't
be paid that period. It carries over to the next one.

- The column header in the file reads Comission, one s. Cosmetic, but it's the

modules.title: Generating your own leads
modules.body_md:
You just saw that a lead you bring in pays 10% instead of 8%, and 13% instead of
10% over $2M. That's because we want to reward you building your own pipeline.

Follow these rules when generating your own leads:

## Leave the professionals to the B2B team

Builders, architects, and designers are handled by our Professional Accounts
team, so leave those relationships to them.

## What's approved, and what isn't

**Approved:** networking with people you know, professional engagement on social
media, and events, like working with an HOA to host an information session for a
neighborhood.

If an event needs funding, put a proposal to the Technology Officer for
approval.

**Not approved:** door-knocking and cold texting. We don't like it when people
do it to us, so we don't do it to anybody else.

## Marketing you make yourself

We'll supply whatever assets you want, print, digital, or physical. You can also
make your own.

**Anything you make yourself goes to the Technology Officer for approval before
you use it.**

Keep the tone positive and educational. "Check out this transformation we just
finished" rather than "DM me for a deal."

## What's off limits

- **Lead hijacking.** You can't claim a lead already in the CRM, or one that
  came from a company-funded source like the website or paid ads
- **Unauthorized incentives.** No discounts outside the stack, no personal
  kickbacks
- **Disparagement.** We win on our own merits. Never take a job by running down
  a competitor
- **Duty interference.** Your own lead generation happens around your scheduled
  work, not instead of it

## Log it right away

Every new lead goes into the CRM as soon as you have it. That's what establishes
it as yours and stops two people working the same person. It's the same habit as
capturing the source on first contact.

modules.title: Andersen series overview
modules.body_md:
Andersen is our number one brand. This is the map of their lines and where each
one fits. Every other Andersen module assumes you know this.

> **Fibrex** is Andersen's own composite, made from wood fiber and polymer. It
> doesn't rot, doesn't need painting, and is 2.5 times stronger than vinyl,
> which lets them build a slimmer frame and more glass. It comes up throughout
> the Andersen line, and the 100 Series gliding door module covers it properly.

## The series

**E-Series.** Architectural collection. Aluminum clad over a wood frame, so no
rot on the exterior. The most versatile line they make.

E-Series is being discontinued. A new 500 Series replaces it, carrying many of
the same features but without some of the heavier customization options. The
transition is expected to start around October 2026, though what Andersen has
told us so far is limited. If a customer mentions the 500 Series, that's what
they mean.

**A-Series.** Fiberglass clad, Fibrex framing, real fiberglass sashes. Built
for coastal and high wind load. Excellent, low volume in our market.

**Big doors.** Moving glass wall systems: bifold, lift and slide, multi-glide.
They need serious wall engineering, minimum 2x6, and won't work on 2x4. That
suits new construction, not replacement. We have sold them to restaurants and
homeowners.

**400 Series.** Andersen's Best category, and our workhorse. Wood interior with
a vinyl clad exterior, mid-price, proven over decades. More on it below.

**200 Series.** Also vinyl clad. Windows use nominal sizing that can't be
customized, so mostly new construction. But the 200 Series sliding glass door
is a top seller and a great product.

**100 Series.** Fibrex composite, no wood at all. Newer, evolving, and we sell
a lot of it. The new 100 Series double hung should become one of our top
sellers over the next decade. Their gliding windows are already our go-to for
screened porch conversions.

### More about the 400 Series

It comes in two windows that share the same frame and differ in materials. The
**Tilt Wash** is vinyl clad wood outside, wood inside. The **Woodwright** is the
same but adds Fibrex to the exterior, which is why it's the upgrade. Because they
share the frame and most specs, moving a customer between them is easy.

Both use traditional wood window sizes, so no custom sizing on the double hungs.
Three interior colors, seven exterior.

## Telling whether it's already an Andersen

Plenty of customers will tell you they have Andersen windows, and believe it, and
be wrong. Sometimes it's what a previous owner said, sometimes it's what the
builder claimed, sometimes it's just that Andersen is the name people know.
Always check for yourself.

From inside the house, look at the lower right corner of the glass. If it's an
Andersen you'll see the **AW logo etched into the glass.** Etched, not a decal,
so it can't be washed or peeled off. On a double hung both sashes carry it.

Andersen has been etching glass since at least September 1962, so this covers
almost anything you'll walk into.

Older than that and it's harder. They sometimes stamped the company name into
hardware, so check the lock. Material helps too, mostly by ruling Andersen out:
**an all vinyl window is never an Andersen.** They have only ever made vinyl clad
wood, which is vinyl outside and wood inside. Vinyl on the inside as well means
it isn't theirs.

[Do I Have Andersen Windows?](https://www.windowworksnc.com/do-i-have-andersen-windows/)
has the full version, and the quiz covers this.

## What we lead with

The full guidance is in The lineup in week 2, but the three most common cases
are worth knowing now.

- **Full frame replacement of standard old wood windows** is the 400 Series
  Tilt Wash
- **The same job on a colonial style house** is the 400 Series Woodwright
- **Insert or replacement windows** are the 100 Series, double hung, casement,
  and so on

## Andersen Aluminum, which we don't sell

**Andersen Aluminum.** Sold only in Arizona, California, New Mexico, Nevada, and
Texas, and built for those climates. Not available here.

## The colors match across every line

**Andersen white is the same white on every series, every style, and every
cladding material.** Same for black, dark bronze, Sandtone, and Terratone.

So you can mix aluminum clad, vinyl clad, and Fibrex in one house and the colors
still match. That's a real selling point when somebody is combining E-Series with
400, or adding 100 Series gliders to a porch.

## How Andersen ranks their own lines

Andersen sorts the series into four tiers, and customers who have been on their
site will have seen this language.

- **Premium.** E-Series and A-Series
- **Best.** 400 Series
- **Better.** 200 Series
- **Good.** 100 Series

Good doesn't mean cheap and it isn't a warning. The 100 Series product statement
is "the smartest alternative to vinyl," and it's the one we sell most of.

**Also worth reading:**
[An In-Depth Comparison of the Different Andersen Window Series](https://www.windowworksnc.com/an-in-depth-comparison-of-the-different-andersen-window-series/).
Colors, hardware finishes, and shapes for every line, and the quiz covers this
one too.

## Why we sell them

Andersen was founded in 1903 and is still family and employee owned rather than
publicly traded. Their customer service is genuinely good, and they stock parts
for windows they stopped making in the 1960s.

Hans Andersen ran a family lumber company in Bayport, Minnesota, bought his
brothers out, and started making windows. Shipping assembled windows was hard,
so he sold frames knocked down for assembly on site and boxed the sashes
separately, then shipped nationally by rail. He also built it as a mass
production line.

They invented the vinyl window in the 1960s, decided it wasn't structurally
sound, and abandoned it. Today they make no all-vinyl window.

The strongest thing you can say is that we have them in our own homes.

modules.title: Setting up Pipedrive
modules.body_md:
Pipedrive is our CRM. Every customer, every deal, and every conversation about
a job lives there, and it's our record of truth. If it isn't in Pipedrive, it
didn't happen.

Two things to set up before you start using it.

## Email sync

Profile, then personal preferences, then email sync. Connect your Window Works
email to your Pipedrive account. Once it's on, emails between you and a
customer attach to their deal automatically and you never update them by hand.

## Profile picture

Also in personal preferences. A photo, a cartoon or memoji, a picture of your
pet, something that represents you, or a graphic of your initials. The
Technology Officer can make you the initials graphic.

It's there so the team can tell at a glance who owns a deal from the pipeline
view, without opening it.

modules.title: Navigating the homeowner pipeline
modules.body_md:
Pipedrive is built on the idea that sales success comes from managing stages and
activities within a pipeline. Stages are the customer's journey: initial
contact, measure scheduled, quote delivered, initial deposit, and on to final
payment. Activities are the things you do to move them along: calls, emails, the
visit.

Most of your work as a B2C salesperson happens in the homeowner pipeline. We
also run pipelines for professional accounts, installation and services, and
soliciting reviews at the end.

Each deal card is a customer. By default you see only the deals you own.

## Card shading

**White** means open and actively being worked.

**Red** means rotting. Each stage has a set amount of time we would expect
between touches. Past that with no interaction, the card turns red.

**Green** means won, and it also gets a green won sticker.

## Activity icons

The small circle on the card, which is different from the card shading.

**Red** is an overdue activity. Something you scheduled didn't get marked
done.

**Yellow** is no next activity scheduled. That's a problem, because we always
want to know what happens next.

**Green** is something due today. Your to-do list.

**Gray** is scheduled for a future date.

**When it's all gray, you're done for the day.** Every deal you own should show
only gray icons when you finish work. Red means an activity is overdue. Yellow
means we don't know what happens next. Green means something today isn't
done.

## Won deals disappearing

Pipedrive is designed for one-and-done sales, so by default a won deal vanishes
from view. That doesn't work for us. If your later stages look empty, or the
installation pipeline looks empty, go to filters and turn on the **All Deals**
filter.

modules.title: Essential customer information
modules.body_md:
Every customer has a person record. Most of the time one already exists by the
time a deal reaches you, and your job is to check it's complete and correct. On
a lead you sourced yourself, you're the one creating it.

Either way, these are the fields that matter.

## Name

First and last, spelled correctly, **capitalized correctly.**

This becomes the name on the contract they sign, so it needs to match who they
actually are. It's also what goes on every appointment reminder and email we
send them. Getting somebody's name wrong is a small rudeness that lands before
you've met them.

Always fine to ask someone to confirm the spelling.

## Phone and email

**Double check the email.** The email sync is defined by the address on the
person record. If it's wrong here, your emails to that customer won't attach to
the deal even when you sent them to the right address. Silent failure, and the
whole thread goes missing for whoever picks the deal up later.

## Address

Needed if we're visiting. The install team plans routes by zip, and we pull this
address for mailers.

**Pipedrive won't show you the zip.** It autocompletes the address, and it knows
the zip, it just doesn't display it. Type a comma after USA, then a 2, and it
fills in. Long-standing bug, so expect it every time you enter an address
yourself.

## How they heard about us

Ask every time it isn't already there.

Leads reach us through several channels, and each one creates the person record
in Pipedrive from whatever the customer typed in. The booking widget, a contact
form, the discount popup, local service ads, and the chatbot. They collect
different amounts of information, so what lands in front of you varies.

The booking widget asks how they heard about us. The popup doesn't, and often
gives you only a phone, email, and first name, sometimes not even a last name.
On those you're gathering the last name, the address, and the source on first
contact.

This helps us keep track of which referral channels are working, and makes sure
we're saying thank you to people who send their friends and neighbors our way.

## About this video

It references Calendly, which we've replaced with our own booking widget. The
mechanism is the same, the name isn't.

modules.title: Moving deals between stages
modules.body_md:
The goal is that Pipedrive reflects what's happening with a customer **in real
time**, because things downstream start moving the moment you update it.

## Why real time matters

Automations fire on stage changes and on activities being scheduled or
completed. If the update is late, the automation is late.

**Schedule the measure activity and the customer immediately gets a welcome
email** thanking them for requesting a consultation, with a teaser of our Ingage
presentation, the slide deck you'll walk customers through in the home, to get
them looking forward to the appointment.

That's why the activity goes in when the appointment is booked, not later. Sent
after the visit has already happened, it arrives thanking somebody for
requesting an appointment they've just had.

**Move a deal to Initial Deposit and it triggers a run of activities** for
admin and project management: moving it to the installation pipeline,
scheduling the final measure, updating payment details, confirming paperwork.
None of that starts until the stage moves.

## Three ways to move a deal

Drag and drop the card in the pipeline view.

Inside the deal, use the compact pipeline strip and click the stage.

Or the same strip in the deal detail. Careful with the dropdown next to it,
that moves the deal to a different **pipeline**, not a different stage.

## The point

You're the one working the deal, but the rest of the team depends on this being
accurate.

## About this video

It shows the welcome email firing when you move the deal to Measure Scheduled.
That changed. It now fires when the measure activity is scheduled. Everything
else in the video still holds.

Rose confirmed 2026-08-09 that rescheduling the measure activity does not fire

modules.title: Effective activity management
modules.body_md:
Stages are where a customer is. Activities are what you do to move them along.
Your scheduled activities are your to do list.

## Setting an activity

Calls, emails, and tasks are simple. Name those whatever makes sense to you.

Some predefined activities aren't yours at all. Final measure belongs to the
project manager, and ordering, order acknowledgments, and scheduling
installations sit with other roles.

You can assign an activity to somebody else. Useful when a customer walks into
the store and a rep needs to follow up.

### The Free in-home sales consultation

This one works differently from the rest, and it's the activity type you'll use
most.

Scheduling a Free in-home sales consultation activity blocks that appointment
time on our measures calendar. That's how we stop more consultations being
booked than we have people to run them, so the activity isn't only your
reminder. It's what protects everybody's day.

**Always capture the time, and capture the end time too.** The calendar treats
the duration as how long you're busy. Set one for 30 minutes when it runs 90 and
somebody can book over you through the website.

When one is set for you, the activity is named with the homeowner's first and
last name and nothing else. **Don't add anything to that subject line.** The
appointment reminder system reads it as the customer's name, so whatever you put
there is what gets texted back to them.

**If you need to move, rename, or reschedule one, come to the Technology Officer
first.** There's more attached to it on the back end than is worth explaining
here, and the new system will handle this better.

## The rule

**Pipedrive should always show what has happened and what will happen next.**

That's the whole discipline. Everything below follows from it.

## Never mark something complete that didn't happen

If a customer cancels, don't mark the appointment done and book another. Now
it looks like two consultations happened.

Delete or edit the activity, then **write a note recording what actually
occurred.** Scheduled for the 17th at 11:30, called on the 15th to cancel.

Then schedule what happens next. Call to reschedule.

## Never leave a completed call with no notes

The note is the only record of what happened on a call. Without one there's no
way to tell whether you reached them, left a message, or what was said.

If a customer calls the store about that conversation, whoever answers has
nothing.

Minimal is fine. "Left voicemail, trying to reschedule measure" does the job. If
you had a real conversation, write more. "Interested in E-Series, coming to the
store to see color samples" tells the next person exactly where things stand.

Three of these are worth the effort even when nobody asks.

**You won't remember.** Five customers and three weeks on, the note is what
tells you which one was waiting on their spouse and which one asked about black
exteriors.

**It settles things.** If a customer says nobody ever called them, the note is
the answer.

**It means fewer questions for you.** When the trail is there, the rest of us
can see a pipeline is being worked without having to ask you about every deal
on it.

If something needs to reach a specific person, though, a note isn't the way to
do it. @ mention them, which the next module covers.

## Your activities view

The calendar icon in the sidebar. Filter by overdue, due today, upcoming, sort
by due date, filter by activity type.

**Worth checking when you close out a deal.** Won and lost deals can leave
future activities behind, and they'll keep showing up as overdue even though
the card is gone from your pipeline view.

modules.title: Internal messaging with @ mentions
modules.body_md:
An @ mention is the fastest way to ask a colleague something about a specific
deal without starting an email chain.

## How

In the deal's **note** section, type @ and it pulls up the team. Start typing a
name and it autocompletes. Write your message and save. They get a notification.

You can pin a note so it stays at the top, useful for something you're holding
until close.

## About this video

It shows @ mentions not working inside an activity. Pipedrive has fixed that
since we filmed, and they work there now.

## What you'll use it for

Anything about a specific deal that needs another person's eyes, and anything
that needs to reach somebody rather than just sit in the record.

Telling the project manager the customer only wants morning installs. Letting
admin know somebody prefers afternoons before they schedule the final measure.
Asking a colleague what an adder covers before you put it in a quote.

Anything for the crew goes through the project manager rather than to them
directly.

The mention notifies the person and the message stays on the deal, so it's still
there for whoever picks the job up later.

They'll come the other way too. Somebody asking what's next on a deal that's
showing the yellow no next activity icon.

Or a heads up with something attached. Say a customer asks about swapping a
single door and two sidelites for a double door. We've just published a post on
why that usually isn't possible. You get an @ mention with the link, to share
with them.

modules.title: Winning and losing a deal
modules.body_md:
## Winning

You mark a deal won in Vendo at the appointment. In Pipedrive it works
differently, because a Pipedrive deal isn't marked won until the money has been
collected, and you're not the one collecting it.

When a customer signs, you'll be emailed a copy of the paperwork. The Vendo
modules cover that side.

**Here, move the deal to Initial Deposit.** That's your part in Pipedrive. It
triggers the run of activities for admin and project management, and it's where
the rest of the team picks the job up.

Admin collects the payment, records it, and marks the Pipedrive deal won. The
card turns green at that point, not before.

## Losing

Click Lost, or drag the card into the lost bucket. Either works.

You'll be asked for a reason. The list is set by admin. If none of them fit what
happened, tell us and we'll add one.

**The reasons, and what each means:**

> Several of these should be rare, because we screen for them before you're sent
> anywhere. Under our minimums, home on the market, outside of scope, and seal
> failure all get checked when the lead comes in. Your time is the thing we're
> protecting.

**Home on the market.** We don't work with real estate agents quoting homes that
are listed. Those are usually negotiating tools and rarely become deals. We're
happy to work with the homeowner once they own it.

**Outside our service area.** Effectively extinct. Our booking widget validates
the address and won't let anyone outside the area book, and admin won't book one
over the phone either. This reason is a relic from before we had an address
validator.

**Under our minimums.** We do our best to qualify leads before sending you out,
so this should be rare. If somebody gets through, or was working around it, try
to convert them to a larger project and help them understand prices only go up.
If they truly need one window, we aren't their company.

**Lead time.** Sometimes their timeline isn't something we can meet. Often this
is education: an Andersen E-Series window takes longer to build than a vinyl
one, and that's production time, not our scheduling.

**Lost to follow-up.** They ghosted us. Try to reignite it first.

**Outside of scope.** They want windows plus siding, or something we don't do.
Try to catch it before the visit, though a popup or online booking may not tell
you.

**Customer gathering info, not ready.** Just getting a sense of cost. Worth
explaining that today's quote is the least they'll ever spend.

**Window Works declines to proceed.** Rare, and a company side decision. Talk to
your manager first, there's usually more going on.

**Seal failure.** We got out there and they don't need new windows.

### More about seal failure

A failed seal is the glass unit, not the window. Air leaks into the space
between the panes, moisture comes with it, and you get fog or haze that wiping
won't shift. The frame and the hardware can be perfectly sound. Often the fix is
replacing the sealed glass unit rather than the whole window, and that's a
different job at a very different price.

Worth reading before you're standing in front of one:
[What to Do About Foggy Windows](https://www.windowworksnc.com/what-to-do-about-foggy-windows/).

### Three that get mixed up

All three end without a sale from us, and the difference is what the customer
did instead. Ask enough questions to tell them apart.

**Cost.** They bought windows, just cheaper somewhere else.

**Materials purchased elsewhere.** They bought windows too, but wanted a Pella
or a Marvin, which we don't carry. Product, not price.

**Decided not to proceed.** They didn't buy at all. Sometimes life happens. We
had a customer ready to sign whose water heater went the same week.

## A lost deal isn't gone

The card turns red and drops out of your open view. **Reopen it any time and
everything is still there.** Nothing is lost.

So there's no harm in marking a deal lost once you have genuinely worked it. If
they call back in three months, click reopen.

modules.title: How our pricing works
modules.body_md:
Every price we quote is built the same way, from cost. This is what sits on top
of it, and what comes off it.

## The multiplier

**Our base is 2.04 times cost.**

The 2.00 is the margin. The 0.04 covers credit card processing, which is why
customers never see a separate card fee. It's already in the number.

**Installation is priced separately, through adders in Vendo.** Some are line
level, attached to an individual window or door. Some are project level, applied
to the job as a whole. Which adders apply, and when, is covered in detail in the
Vendo modules.

You aren't doing this math yourself. The quoting systems apply it, and the
modules on each one cover how.

**We don't go below the margin.** Everything below is a discount off the
2.04, not a change to it.

## Tax

**Tax applies to products, not to labor.** Rate is 7.25% in Wake County.

That includes rot repair.

Each quoting system handles tax slightly differently and a couple have
exceptions. These will be covered in detail in the module for each
manufacturer's quoting process.

## The discount stack

Two tiers, and they work differently.

**Applied directly to the multiplier:**

- **Three day deal.** 5% if they commit within three days.
- **Cash discount.** 8% if they're paying cash rather than financing.
- **Referral bonus.** $100 flat if a friend or neighbor sent them.

**Applied through the margin alignment factor:**

Some customers arrive expecting a specific discount. Someone who filled in a
popup offering 20% off their project is going to want to see that 20% come off,
and they should.

The margin alignment factor is how you show it. Add the factor first, which
raises the price 11.11%, then apply either the **10% or the 5% authorized
discount.** Not both. The customer sees the discount they were promised, and
because the factor and the discount roughly offset, the final number still sits
above our floor.

It has to go in before you build the quote, not after.

**Past 20% total, you hit a wall.** Vendo requires authorization and texts
leadership. They'll want to know what the deal needs, so come with the reason
rather than just the number.

One thing to watch: on a low value deal, the flat $100 referral can be enough to
push the total past 20% and trigger approval when nothing else would. That one
gets approved, it just has to be routed.

## Financing

Three options through Synchrony Bank:

- 18 months deferred interest. Interest accrues from day one and is written off
  entirely if the balance is paid in full before the 18 months are up. Miss that
  date and the whole accrued amount is charged at once, which is why we never
  describe this as no interest
- 10.99% APR until paid in full
- 5.99% APR until paid in full

Preapproval is required before an order is placed. **Financed orders collect no
deposit.**

The customer facing version of all this is on our
[financing page](https://www.windowworksnc.com/financing/), which is worth
reading so you're saying the same thing the website says.

Present these in the Price Kit. Enter the project total and it shows monthly
figures alongside the cash option.

## Deposit and payment

**50% deposit, then 50% on completion.** Financed orders collect no deposit.

The Project Manager collects the deposit at the Measurement Confirmation
appointment. Admin handles logging it, so you don't enter payments anywhere.

What you do need is to be able to explain the terms clearly at the table, because
a customer who understands them upfront doesn't argue about them later.

- They'll pay the Project Manager, not you
- We don't accept cash or checks by mail
- Card is Visa, Mastercard, Discover, or American Express, and we can take it in
  person or over the phone
- If they'd rather pay by check, the PM takes it at the final measure, or comes
  back for it

**All sales are final.** No returns, refunds, or exchanges. Say this plainly
rather than letting a customer discover it later.

## When a job has to be staged

**Set this expectation at the table, on every job.**

Two different things get called splitting a project up, and they are not the
same.

**Phased** is a customer choosing to order some of their windows now and the rest
later, to spread the cost. That's their decision, and the buying guide explains
why it usually ends up costing them more.

**Staged** is us having to break the installation across more than one visit,
because a unit arrived damaged or the manufacturer backordered something. That's
a manufacturing or shipping problem, outside our control and nobody's choice.

**When a job is staged, we bill for the work as it's completed.** We invoice for
what's finished and payment is expected then, and the rest is invoiced when the
rest is done.

A project counts as complete once all the windows and doors are installed. Small
outstanding items that don't need further installation work, a screen still in
transit for example, don't hold up that invoice. We deliver or fit those as soon
as they arrive.

For your own understanding rather than something to explain at the table: on
small outstanding items like a damaged screen or sash, the PM may authorize
holding back a small amount from the final balance. You don't need to raise that
with a customer, but you should know it exists.

Customers who hear about staging for the first time at the end of a job feel
ambushed. Customers who heard it during the quote treat it as normal, which it
is.

## What the customer already knows

**Our average project is $22,745.** That's the mean since 2021, and it's
published, so plenty of customers arrive already knowing it. Projects run from
about $7,000 to $100,000. Under $10,000 is unlikely for a whole house, and a
large job with high efficiency demands and premium materials can pass $50,000.

Two things worth doing before your first appointment. Go to our
[pricing page](https://www.windowworksnc.com/pricing/) and play with the slider,
which is what a customer will have done. And read the
[Guide to Buying Windows](window-buying-guide.pdf), which is what we send them
when they book. Between them you'll know what a customer has already been told
before you walk in.

Our minimum is **three windows or one door** per job. Service area is a
30-mile radius from Cary.

## What isn't in the price

Rot repair. It's excluded from every quote. If rot is found, the PM assesses it
and a signed change order is required before any repair goes ahead.

If you can see it coming, say so at the table. Soft trim, peeling paint, staining
under a sill, a window that's been leaking. Tell them what you're looking at, that
we won't know the extent until the old unit is out, and that if there is rot the
PM will price it and they'll sign off before anyone touches it. A customer who
was warned treats a change order as expected. A customer who wasn't treats it as
a bait and switch.

Painting is optional and priced separately. Standard service means primed trim
only, with visible nail holes, and the customer does the sanding, filling, and
top coat. Painting service means we do it. It must be discussed during the
quote because they sign off on it in the installation agreement. If neither box
is checked, standard applies.

A Porta-John, at roughly $350 a week, if a customer won't provide restroom
access. This has come up once in twenty years, so it's a line you mention while
going through the installation agreement rather than something to raise.

modules.title: The lineup, and what to lead with
modules.body_md:
What you lead with is decided by a few things: what's already in the house, the
install type it needs, the style of the home, and anything specific the customer
has their heart set on. Green windows narrow it to a couple of lines before
you've considered anything else.

Which is why the needs assessment comes first. Get it right and this module
answers the rest for you.

**Quote a standard size wherever one exists.** Custom costs more, so if the
opening can take a standard size, that's what goes in the quote. Custom is for openings where nothing standard fits.

**One rule before anything else: don't quote two or three different window
lines.** It creates confusion, the customer freezes, and then someone else
walks in with one window and one price and wins. Pick the right line and lead
with it.

## A. Existing old wood windows

**Full frame, standard** → Andersen 400 Series Tilt Wash

**Full frame, colonial home or they want a fiberglass composite exterior** →
Andersen 400 Series Woodwright, as the upgrade

Both use traditional wood window sizes, so no custom sizing. They share sizes
and many specs, so moving a customer between them is easy.

400 Series picture windows can be quoted to match, but note they're custom
sized. Picture windows don't follow traditional wood sizes even though the
double hungs do.

**Full frame casement** → Andersen 100 Series or 400 Series

100 Series if they want fully fiberglass composite, and it costs less. 400 Series
if they want a wood interior.

Either way, casements get custom sized. That's true whether you're replacing
a double hung or an existing casement.

**Insert or replacement** → Andersen 100 Series double hung, casement, picture,
or gliding

This is the preferred option and a much better solution than vinyl. Lead with
it.

**Insert or replacement, vinyl option** → Vinyl Design Mountainview 1000, in
double hung, casement, picture, or gliding

## B. Existing vinyl windows

Remember this is always full frame vinyl. There's no wood frame to insert
into.

**Full frame** → Andersen 100 Series
**Full frame, vinyl option** → Vinyl Design

**Two things to check every time on a vinyl-to-vinyl job:**

**J-channel.** Verify the siding type and whether the new windows need one.
Vinyl windows offer J-channel as an integral, optional part of the frame.
Andersen does not, so it has to be sourced locally as additional material.

**Interior trim.** Do the existing windows use extension jambs or drywall
returns, and what depth? That determines whether you need interior cutbacks,
stops, or both.

## C. Entry and hinged doors

**Hinged patio doors** → Andersen E-Series, aluminum clad, or A-Series,
fiberglass

Unless you're specifically selling an all-fiberglass option, lead with these.
Both offer standard and custom sizes, traditional and contemporary styles, and
sizes you can't get in other lines or brands.

**Hinged entry doors,** including front doors, single entry, and fire-rated →
ProVia, any series

Lead with fiberglass. It's more wear resistant than steel, though their steel
doors are well made.

Andersen does make an entry door. We don't recommend it to most homeowners: the
options are extremely limited and you'll sell a fiberglass door almost every
time. We sell approximately one every two to three years.

## D. Gliding doors

**Two panel:**

| Line | Material | Style | Price |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 Series | Fiberglass composite | Contemporary | Most competitive |
| 400 Series | Vinyl clad | Traditional panels | Moderate |
| 200 Series | Vinyl clad | Contemporary, a few more options | Moderate |
| A-Series / E-Series | Fiberglass / aluminum clad | Both, highly customizable | Higher |

**Four panel:** same as above, minus the 100 Series. It only comes as a two
panel.

## E. Specialty doors

**Moving glass wall systems,** outswing bifold, multi-glide, lift and slide →
Andersen Big Doors

These run roughly **$1,700 to $2,300 per linear foot for the door alone,** before
labor or any wall work. So a 16 foot opening lands in the tens of thousands. That
number is worth knowing early, because it tells you fairly quickly whether you're
in a real conversation or an idle one, and you can find that out without making
the customer feel judged for asking.

They're custom only and need a minimum 2x6 wall, so they won't go into a 2x4.
Quoting one takes a week or two and involves an engineer and a site visit, which
means you're not pricing it at the table.

What you do at the appointment is recognize what they're asking for, tell them
what the process looks like and roughly what it costs, and hand it to the COO.
It goes from there to the engineer, the site visit, and confirming the build with
Andersen.

If they're also buying windows, quote the windows as their own package so the
whole job isn't waiting on the door.

**They want the wide open feel without the price** → 200 Series, 400 Series, or
E-Series four panel gliding doors

These customize to around 16 feet and cost far less. We never use the word cheap.
More economical, less expensive.

## F. Specialty windows

**Architectural shapes,** half circles, trapezoids, rectangles, arches,
springlines → Andersen ASW

Almost always full frame. Always custom sized, regardless of brand or series.

modules.title: Using Vendo: navigation, adders, and final documents
modules.body_md:
This module covers the appointment flow, from adders through to the customer
signing.

## Starting the appointment

Your appointment should already be waiting for you, sent over from Pipedrive. If
it isn't, create one with the plus sign in the lower right.

For an existing customer, search and select them. For a new one, add them. **Capitalize the names.**
They pull into documentation if this becomes a win.

Additional contact adds a spouse or a contractor who needs to be on the
paperwork.

Vendo pulls in the property value, year built, and house size once you enter
the address.

**Don't hit Start until you know you'll be quoting them that day.** Once a
deal starts you have to result it as won, lost, or pending. If nobody is home
or they cancel at the door, don't start it.

## Needs assessment

There are eleven questions, and **they're ours rather than Vendo's defaults.** Order doesn't
matter, and if you get the answers through normal conversation that's better.
It's an internal document to make sure you covered the bases.

- Windows, doors, or both
- Whether they've had replacement work done before
- Their reasons for considering it
- Age of the existing units
- Energy efficiency goals
- Whether they want a style change
- UV protection for furniture and flooring
- Project timing
- HOA guidelines
- Any questions about the installation itself

**The most important one is whether they've ever had window or door
replacement done before.** Most people have not. They have put it off for
years, and there's usually real sticker shock and no familiarity with the
terms, including something as basic as full frame versus pocket insert.

You're gauging how much they already know about window and door replacement, and
then meeting them at that level.

Also worth setting early: this is a construction project. There will be dust and
debris. We clean it up, but people who weren't expecting it get upset on day one
of their installation.

## The flow

Inspection and Configure do two different jobs. **Inspection** records the state
of the windows they already have, which is useful information to give a customer.
**Configure** is where you build the new ones.

**Use Configure Now and build each window as you measure it,** room by room.
Don't collect all the measurements and then sit down to quote, it takes far
longer and you end up camped in someone's house.

## Demo

There are three tiles. **Open the blue Ingage one** to present. The black one with the
suitcase is only there so Vendo can email them a link at the end. The third is
Price Kit, and you come back to it after the quote to show financing.

Load the presentation before the appointment so it opens fast.

## Configure

Build the windows and doors. Andersen is directly integrated because Vendo is a
Paradigm product and Paradigm built Andersen Access. Reeb, the distributor we buy Therma-Tru
doors from, and ProVia both import by quote number. Vinyl Design doesn't integrate and needs the workaround.

Building Andersen windows in detail has its own module, next.

**Adders.** An adder is anything that isn't the window itself: the labor to install
it, the materials around it, and any extra work the job needs. They're how
installation gets priced, so a quote with the right window and the wrong adders is
still a wrong quote.

There are two kinds. **Line level** adders sit inside an individual Andersen line
item, because they apply to that one unit. **Project level** adders sit at the
end, because they apply to the whole job. The margin alignment factor goes in
first, before anything else.

Understanding project adders in Vendo covers which adders exist and when each
applies. Adder traps covers the ones that go wrong.

## Quote and price kit

Take the project total into the Price Kit under Demo and enter it as the
project total. That shows them the cash number alongside the three Synchrony
financing options with monthly figures.

The three dots in the upper right apply discounts, which the pricing module
covers. Anything over 20 percent triggers an approval text to leadership.

Bring the discounts back into Vendo on the quote screen.

## Documents

Hit Proceed. Two documents are required and pre-selected, so you can't deselect
them.

**Installation agreement.** Estimate the duration in days and describe the units
in plain words. You'll also fill in the moulding application, the casings,
whether or not there's a back band, the exterior casing, and quantities for sill
nosing replacement, storm window removal, and affixing window treatments.

Talk them through it rather than letting them read it cold. The things that
cause problems later are all in here:

- Rot repair isn't included. If we find it, the PM assesses and a signed
  change order is required before repairs proceed.
- We don't reinstall or calibrate security systems, or program smart locks and
  keypads.
- We don't guarantee existing blinds, curtains, shutters, or shades will fit
  the new windows. They can come to the showroom and check.
- We don't reuse existing mouldings or casings. They're usually brittle and
  removing them intact isn't worth the carpentry.
- If they bought their own door hardware, it has to be compatible and ready on
  install day. We can't fit a dummy handle, the strike plate won't line up,
  and the door can't be secured.
- Painting. Standard service means primed trim and visible nail holes, and they
  do the sanding and painting themselves. Painting service means we do it, and
  it has to have been in the quote as an adder. **We don't offer staining at
  all**, so if they want stained trim they'll be arranging that themselves.
- Restroom access. This has come up once in twenty years, but if they won't
  designate one we coordinate a Porta-John at roughly $350 a week at their
  expense.
- The final walkthrough happens within 48 hours of completion.
- Window Works offers a two year warranty on workmanship for products we
  install, beginning from the date of installation. Manufacturer defects,
  including seal failure and hardware, go through the manufacturer.

**Payment policy.** Check how the customer plans to pay: cash, check, card, or
financing. Then talk through the middle section. A project counts as complete
once all windows and doors are installed,
even if a screen hasn't arrived or a damaged sash is being replaced. Payment
is due then. Set that expectation now rather than arguing about it later.

## Signing

Ask how they want to sign. **On this device right now** is the one call close
and what you want. Personal device means they want to think about it or talk to
a spouse who isn't there.

Hand them the iPad. They review, agree to the electronic signature consent, and
initial and sign. Drawn or typed both work.

They hand it back, you hit proceed.

## Sending

Hit Finish and both signed contracts go out automatically. The customer gets
their documents, and leadership, admin, operations, and the project manager get
everything they need to start scheduling the final measure and ordering.

You can add the inspection report, useful if there was a lot of damage, and the
Ingage presentation if the customer asked for it.

**You mark the deal won in Vendo,** and you need to. That's separate from
Pipedrive, where admin marks it won once the money has actually been collected.
Two systems, two different moments.

While Vendo has the option to add photographs, we don't use their native system,
as it's limited to storing only ten photos. We use CompanyCam for project photos,
and that's covered in detail in a later module.

## If they don't sign

Result the deal as pending or lost. Don't leave it open.

## About this video

It says the Pipedrive appointment automation is still being worked out. That's
resolved, and appointments preload now.

The payment policy has also changed since filming. You now select how the
customer intends to pay.

And when it was filmed we were in the North-Central ENERGY STAR zone. We're now
South-Central. Vendo is locked to our zone, so it isn't a question you have to
answer.
