modules.title: Quoting Andersen windows in Vendo
modules.body_md:
This module covers building the product. The appointment flow and the close are
in the Using Vendo module.

Vendo is a Paradigm product and Paradigm also built the Andersen Access quoting
software, which is why Andersen is directly integrated and ProVia and
Therma-Tru aren't.

## Inspection versus Configure

These do two different jobs. **Inspection** is where you record the state of the
windows they already have, which is useful information to give a customer.
**Configure** is where you build the new ones. Inspection's Save carries your
notes forward but doesn't quote anything.

**Use Configure Now and build each window as you measure it,** room by room.
Don't collect all the measurements and then sit down to quote, because it takes
far longer and you end up camped in someone's house.

One quirk: if you pick double hung in the inspection notes, Configure will only
offer you double hungs. Coming in through Configure directly gives you
everything.

## What not to quote

The product list Vendo shows you includes plenty we don't sell, so **ignore
garden windows and hopper windows entirely.**

Four more to skip in the double hung list:

- **200 Series Tilt Wash** is a new construction window, so it's off the table
  for a replacement job
- **E-Series sash replacement kits,** and sash kits in general, we never sell
- **The Narrowline to Tilt Wash conversion kit** applies so rarely that you can
  assume it doesn't
- **StormWatch and the coastal DP50 or impact options** are built for genuinely
  coastal work. They cost twice as much and weigh twice as much

## Building a window

Installation method: nailing flange for new construction.

Sizing shows you the unit dimension and the rough opening alongside the sash
size. The unit is bigger than the sash by roughly three quarters of an inch for
the frame, and the RO is bigger again for shims and insulation.

Equal sash, cottage, or reverse cottage. You can see which a house has from
outside.

Colors, jamb liner color (gray by default if the window is black), glass.
**Low-E4 SmartSun is our default for this market.** Standard Low-E4 is already
efficient out of the box. HeatLock works well but is designed for northern
climates.

Tempered where code requires it. The
[Tempered glass and code](module:REF-050) reference sheet covers when.

Grilles: full divided light, simulated divided light, removable interior, or
Finelight which is Andersen's between the glass. Match what the customer has,
including the bar width, and get as close as Andersen offers. There's no
industry standard and no custom widths.

If the default pattern isn't what they have, use specified equal light and
enter the custom pattern. Two wide by two high gives you a four over four.

Sash lifts: none on the Tilt Wash. Hardware traditional unless they want
estate.

**Full screen, always.** Andersen charges the same for a half screen as a full
one. TruScene is a real upsell and customers love it.

Extension jambs if it isn't a 2x4 wall. Andersen full frame windows are
4-9/16" and reach the interior on a 2x4. 6-9/16" for a 2x6, 5-1/4" for old plaster
walls.

**Stool: none.** We source our own locally.

## The advanced tab

**We're in the South-Central ENERGY STAR climate zone.** See the correction
note below.

Sizing method: Unicode standard for most old wood double hungs, custom only if
you need it.

Specialty glass, mostly bathroom privacy, and each option prices differently
because it's based on glass area.

High altitude: no. We're a couple of hundred feet.

Gas filled goes to argon automatically. Simulated check rail: no.

Grille colors, exterior and interior, two tone if the window is.

DP upgrade: no, that's coastal.

**Window opening control devices.** Code triggers when a window is 18 inches or
less from the floor with more than a 60 inch drop outside. Screwed in, factory
or field applied. Most people don't want them, but offer them to a family with
small children.

Exterior trim: no. We use PVC, and Andersen's doesn't work in brick.

Room location, then save.

## Saving time

**Copy** creates a new opening with the same configuration. Rooms repeat,
especially upstairs, so this saves real time. Update the quantity if there are
two identical units in one room.

Copying within Configure asks whether to bring your previous choices across.
Say yes, and it carries glass, color, hardware, and screens.

**Copy doesn't bring the adders.** Every copied unit needs its adders added
separately. This is the easiest thing in Vendo to miss, because the copy looks
finished. Missing them means we install a window for free, and there's real labor and
material in that.

## Mulling

Copy and mull, or mull new unit, then pick the location: top, sides, bottom.

Mulling location means where it gets assembled. **Andersen at the factory** for
most things. Field for very large or unusual configurations, which our crews
can handle.

Mull material: one eighth non-reinforced is fine for a typical twin. 3/16 steel
for heavier work.

**V-notch: always no.**

Half circles and other complementary shapes mull on top. Grille patterns on
half circles are fiddly and there are a lot of options.

Trimstop on the inside: yes. Grille alignment: usually yes on transoms and half
circles, no when the geometry doesn't allow it. Drip cap: yes, flexible white.
**Arch casing: none.** We use flex moulding bought locally.

## About this video

At around 26:50 the narrator says we're in the North-Central ENERGY STAR zone,
recently changed from South-Central. He had it the wrong way round. **We're in
South-Central,** changed from North-Central. Vendo is now locked to our zone, so
it's selected for you and isn't a question you answer.

## Where the adders go

Inside the window itself. Configure, Edit, then the Adders tab. Not at project
level, because Andersen is directly integrated.

Full detail is in the Understanding project adders in Vendo module, and in the
Adder traps reference sheet.
modules.author_note:
Rose watched this back 2026-08-09. The narrator simply transposed the two zones
at 26:50, saying north changed from south when he meant south changed from north.
Not being refilmed. There's a note in the module telling the reader.

South-Central criteria: U-Factor 0.28 or lower, SHGC 0.23 or lower. The Most
Efficient tier at U 0.20 or lower is what qualifies for federal tax credits.

modules.title: Quoting Andersen doors in Vendo
modules.body_md:
This module covers building Andersen patio and hinged doors. Go to Configure,
then the **Patio Doors** tab rather than Windows, then the plus sign.

The list is long and repetitive, because it holds hinged and sliding doors with
sidelight and transom options across every Andersen series.

**Faster way to find something:** use the product type filter. Choose gliding
patio door and it narrows immediately. Scrolling for a door while a customer
watches isn't a good look.

## The height rule, and it's the one that costs money

Andersen offers 6'8", 6'11", and 8'0".

**If you're replacing an existing standard door, choose 6'11".** Unit size is
82-3/8", rough opening 83.

Their 6'8" is undersized and won't fit.

Here's the part that confuses people. On a Therma-Tru or ProVia you would
choose **their** 6'8", because for them that's the bigger size. Those
manufacturers size by panel plus frame. Andersen sizes the entire unit. Same
words, different meaning.

## Traditional versus contemporary

Traditional, also called French wood, has wider framing around the glass.
Contemporary has less framing and a cleaner look.

More people are choosing contemporary on hinged doors lately, but traditional
is still a real option. Same quality either way. Walk the customer through it.

## Configuration, viewed from the exterior

**Active left passive right,** or the reverse, or configurations where one
panel is fixed, or both are fixed.

The **active** door is the everyday door and opens first. The **passive** door
opens second and only after the active one is open.

## Colors and wood species

You can split the color, black outside and white inside for example.

Interior is pine, oak, maple, cherry, or mahogany.

**Never choose a high-end wood species and then paint over it.** There's no
point putting white paint on mahogany. Andersen sometimes allows the
combination and sometimes removes it. If it's available, don't take it.
Species upgrades are for staining or leaving unfinished. If it's getting
painted, choose pine.

## Glass

Dual pane, Low-E SmartSun as our default.

**STC glass is sound control,** and it's worth offering. It's the right call for
a customer on a busy road, backing onto a highway, or in a downtown condo. It's
an upcharge and it makes a real difference.

Reveal spacers default to stainless steel, with black and white available.

Grilles are increasingly rare on doors. Most people want the view.

## Hardware, and this is a hard boundary

Every style is a different price. FSB and Ashley Norton are upcharges,
especially on a double door where there's a handle set on each side. Even the
standard Andersen options aren't cheap.

**You must use Andersen hardware.** The multi-point lock is built into the
door.

If a customer doesn't like any of the options, the answer is no, and **we can't
point them anywhere else.** This is what Andersen offers and what we install.

If they buy hardware elsewhere, **we won't fit it.** It isn't part of the
installation and we can't take responsibility for how the door operates
afterwards. They're welcome to arrange that themselves.

**Split finish** lets you run different styles or colors inside and out, which
pairs well with a split color door.

**Finishes are specific to each hardware style, not a universal palette.**
Anvers, for example, only comes in satin nickel, oil rubbed bronze, and bright
brass. If a customer insists on bright brass, you have to work out which sets
offer it.

## Key locks aren't included

**They're always an add-on with Andersen. Never a default.**

**Ask every single time.** Customers routinely assume a key lock is included. It
isn't, so if they want one it has to go on the order.

They can cost upwards of a hundred dollars, which is a reason to raise it at the
table rather than after the door is built.

Keying it to match the rest of the house is locksmith work, and not something we
handle.

## Screens

Unlike windows, doors don't default to a screen.

Andersen's hinged door screen is a double hinged arrangement and it's odd.
**Probably don't offer it.** If a customer wants a screen on a hinged door, a
phantom screen is the better answer.

## The advanced tab

PG upgrade: no in this market.

Unit code `FWHID` is French wood hinged in-swing door, and 60611 is the size.
The swing is baked into the product you select, unlike Reeb where the software
asks you during the quote.

**Frame depth: 4-9/16" for a 2x4, 6-9/16" for a 2x6. This can't be changed
later.** Get it wrong and we're ordering a new door, or at minimum a new
frame, with all the cost and labor that carries. Check the wall depth. This
applies to windows too.

Sill: gray or bronze appearance. **Andersen doesn't offer a mill or aluminum
finish sill.**

Remodel sill bracket: no. Our crews supply whatever support the door needs.

Glass stop profile: chamfer is the automatic default on a traditional door,
ovolo is the alternative.

Threshold: none. Oak and maple are available, they're expensive, and we supply
them in the field.

Specialty glass: usually none. Privacy glass on a back patio door is rare,
front doors are a different conversation.

High altitude: none.

**Hinged doors are always factory assembled.** No option. Every Andersen hinged
door arrives pre-hung in the frame. Gliding doors are a different story, below.

Then hardware styles come back for the split finish, along with hinge color,
panel stop finish, temporary construction hardware (no, the doors ship with an
allen key that locks them), corrosion resistant locking mechanism (coastal
only), and exterior trim (none, we supply our own).

## Gliding doors: always unassembled

**With the exception of the 100 Series, which has no option, every Andersen
two panel patio door can be ordered factory assembled or unassembled. Always
choose unassembled.**

Four reasons:

It is **$100 to $200 less expensive**, which makes us more competitive.

Each panel and the frame are wrapped separately, so **one person can move and
deliver it** and it's far less prone to damage. Assembled, even a five or six
foot door is heavy and awkward.

It is **pre-drilled**. Our crews assemble the frame in 15 to 20 minutes with
the supplied screws and silicone.

And it is **easier to install**, because they can lift the frame into the
opening and build the door on site rather than wrestling a finished unit.

## The auxiliary foot lock isn't optional

It defaults to none. **You choose one anyway, every time.**

Every Andersen sliding door we sell gets a foot lock. It acts as a deadbolt,
sitting at the bottom of the operating panel and locking into the frame. The
cost is minimal, and customers who didn't know they wanted one want it as soon
as you show it to them.

We don't present it as an option. Match the finish to the interior color.

## The 200 Series Narrowline

Worth knowing specifically, because **we sell more of this gliding door than
anything else.** Contemporary profile, available as one, two, or four panel.

Aluminum or gray appearance. **No bronze on this door.**

## Four panel gliders

Two middle panels open into a wide opening, the two ends are fixed. A genuinely
economical alternative to a bifold or multi-glide.

**Stock sizes run 10 feet to 16 feet,** which is 117 to 189 inches. It
customizes in eighth inch increments for odd openings, **but check the stock
sizes first because they're considerably less money.** You can't go below 117
or above 189.

8 foot heights are popular here.

**Two foot locks on a four panel,** because there are two operating panels. On
this door they're close to essential: without them, operating one panel makes
the other move, and most people want one locked in place as the everyday door.

**Four panel doors only come unassembled.** There's no choice. Assembled you
would need a crane.

## Adders

Don't forget them. Patio door adders live inside the line item like windows.

Double door, single with two sidelights, four panel glider, whichever matches.

Add painting if the customer wants the trim painted. On a four panel, the
painting adder is the double door line at **quantity 2.**

modules.title: Install types
modules.body_md:
There are three ways we put a window in, and they carry different labor,
different materials, and different prices.

You settle this at the appointment, before you build anything, because it decides
what the job costs and what you're able to offer the customer. It also answers the
first question most homeowners ask, which is what's actually going to happen to
their house.

For the customer-facing version of this, we have a post on
[full frame versus insert replacement](https://www.windowworksnc.com/full-frame-replacement-vs-insert-replacement-windows/)
with a printable one page comparison you can leave with them.

## Replacement, also called insert or pocket

Customers and other companies also call it a pocket replacement or frame in
frame.

The old wood window frame stays. We take out the upper sash, the lower sash, and
the jamb liners, which are the tracks running up the sides. A smaller window gets
made to fit inside what's left. It's less labor and less material, with no
exterior work in most cases.

**What stays:** the existing frame, and the interior and exterior casing.

**What comes out:** the sashes and the hardware, and nothing else.

### When it's the right call

Medium to large windows with structurally sound frames, meaning no energy
efficiency or moisture concerns. Around here that's usually older wood windows.

It works in any style, so casements, picture windows, and double hungs are all
fine.

The trim staying put is worth naming at the table. A customer with custom trim work, or
wallpaper they don't want disturbed, will care about that more than the price
difference.

### When it isn't

Anywhere rot is known or suspected, or where the window is warping or not
operating properly.

Very small windows, a dormer for example, because the new unit is smaller than
what came out and the reduced glass area looks wrong.

And it's worth being honest about a real limitation: because the frame stays, the
crew has far less access to the wall around the window. They can't assess for rot
back there, and they can't shim or re-insulate the existing frame without taking
the exterior casing off. So an insert on a window you're unsure about can turn
into a change order.

## Full frame

Also called a total tear out or a complete replacement.

The window comes out down to the wall studs, casing and framing with it, and
sometimes some exterior siding. New mouldings inside and out. Nothing of the
original window remains, so every material is new.

Much more labor, much higher material cost, and more days on site.

### What it lets you offer

**A different window.** Size, style, color, and material are all open, so a small
white single hung can become a large black picture window. None of that is
possible on an insert.

**A properly set window.** The crew can shim it plumb, level and square, and add
insulation around it, which is where the energy performance actually comes from.

**A rot resistant exterior**, so the problem they're replacing doesn't come back.

### When it's the right call

Rot known or suspected. A window that isn't operating properly, or is simply old
and breaking down. Or a customer who wants a different look than what's there.

There's no case where full frame is the wrong technical choice. The only argument
against it is cost and time.

## New construction

The opening is already framed and ready. We set the window, shim it plumb level
and square, caulk it, and leave. No trim work inside or out.

Significantly cheaper than either of the others. This is contractor and builder
work where someone else handles the finish. In-home sales rarely sees it. B2B
sees it regularly.

## Two traps

**The screened porch conversion.** It looks like new construction, because
there's an opening waiting for a window. But we're doing trim work and
finishing, so it's full frame. Getting this one wrong is expensive, because
new construction pricing is far below full frame.

**Existing vinyl windows.** If the existing window is all vinyl with no wood
anywhere, and there's J-channel outside with the siding tucked behind it, that
is **full frame vinyl. Always.** It doesn't matter what goes back in. Not an
insert, even if you're putting in an Andersen 100 Series or a ProVia or a
Vinyl Design unit. There's no wood frame to insert into.

## Quick test

Start with the frame. **Is there an existing wood frame we're leaving in place?**
If yes, it's a replacement. If not, keep going.

Then the trim. **Are we trimming it out, or is someone else handling the
finish?** If we're only setting the unit and somebody else finishes it, that's
new construction. If we're doing the trim, it's full frame.

quiz.q: Old wood double hungs, frames are sound, no moisture concerns, and the customer doesn't want her hand-painted trim disturbed. Which install type?
options: Replacement, and the trim stays put
Full frame, for the better install
Full frame, then reuse her original trim
Either one, depending on budget

Replacement, that's what the 100 Series is for

Dormers are always full frame

modules.title: Tempered glass and code
modules.body_md:
Tempered is safety glass. It breaks like a windshield, into small squares
rather than shards, so it's far less likely to cut someone. It's also
stronger than annealed glass, so in many cases it doesn't break at all.

Getting this wrong is the one product mistake with real liability attached.

## Doors: always tempered, no decision to make

**All door glass is tempered by federal law.** Every manufacturer, every size,
from a small decorative lite to a full sheet. Andersen, ProVia, Therma-Tru, all
of them.

You don't select it. You don't quote it as an upgrade. It's simply always
there.

## Windows: know the triggers

Tempered is required when the glass is:

- **18 inches or less from the floor and more than 9 square feet**
- **60 inches or less above a stair, a landing, or the walking surface**
- **60 inches or less inside a shower or tub area**
- **In the path of a door that swings into it**

On a double hung, **the upper and lower sashes count separately.** One sash can
require tempering when the other does not.

## Why it matters when nobody is checking

Replacement windows don't require permits, so there's no inspector coming.
Nothing forces the issue.

Two exposures remain.

**Injury.** Someone falls on the stairs or slips in the shower and goes through
the glass. Untempered glass in those locations is exactly the scenario the code
exists to prevent.

**Resale.** An inspector during a future sale catches untempered glass where
code requires it. That's a call from a former customer two years later, and a
problem they now have to fix.

Know the code and temper where it belongs, even though nobody will check at the
time.

## Don't confuse this with window opening control devices

Different rule, different purpose. Those are about children falling out of
windows.

**Required when the window is 18 inches or less from the floor and the outside
drop is more than 60 inches.**

They screw into the window and can be factory or field applied. Most people don't want them. Not strictly required on a replacement where no permit is
pulled, but worth offering to a family with small children.

quiz.q: A customer asks whether the glass in their new front door will be tempered. What do you tell them?
options: Always. All door glass is tempered by federal law, every brand and every size.
Only if they pay for the upgrade
Only on doors with large glass panels
Only on doors near a walking surface

quiz.q: A picture window sits 14 inches off the floor and is about 12 square feet. Does it need tempering?
options: No, it isn't near a door or stairs
Only if there are children in the home
Yes. Under 18 inches from the floor and over 9 square feet.
Only if a permit is pulled

A double hung in a second floor bedroom, 30 inches off the floor, 8 square feet
A window in a tub surround 40 inches up
A window a door swings into

options: It's cheaper to temper everything
Manufacturers won't ship untempered glass
It isn't necessary without a permit

quiz.q: A window is 16 inches off the floor with a 10 foot drop outside. What's triggered?
options: Tempered glass
A window opening control device
Both automatically
Neither

modules.title: Egress and sleeping rooms
modules.body_md:
Egress means a way out. Code requires every sleeping room to have one, big enough
for somebody to climb out of in a fire and for a firefighter to climb in and back
out wearing full gear, including the air pack on their back. That air pack is a
large part of why the opening has to be as wide as it is.

There's no such thing as an egress window as a product. It's an ordinary window
that opens wide enough to meet code.

Every room used for sleeping has to have an emergency way out. That isn't only rooms labeled
bedroom on a plan. A bonus room over the garage, a converted office, a nursery, a
teenager's flex room. If somebody sleeps in it, it needs a way out.

A picture window is fixed, so its clear opening is zero and it can never satisfy
egress on its own. But the code requires an escape opening, not specifically a
window, so a picture window is fine in a sleeping room as long as something else
in that room provides the way out.

**What counts:** another window that opens wide enough, or a door that leads
directly outside to a yard or a path to the street. A door into a hallway doesn't
count.

## The North Carolina numbers

Worth knowing, because they aren't the national figures. Most guides online quote
the generic model code, and our inspectors enforce something different.

North Carolina measures the **clear opening**, meaning the actual hole once the
window is open rather than the size of the glass. A window in a sleeping room has
to meet all of these:

- At least **4 square feet** of net clear opening
- At least **22 inches** of net clear opening height
- At least **20 inches** of net clear opening width
- A sill no higher than **44 inches** from the floor

On top of that there's a minimum glass size: at least 5 square feet of glazing on
a ground floor window, and at least 5.7 square feet upstairs.

**A big window can still fail** if it doesn't open far enough, because what gets
measured is the hole rather than the glass.

## On a replacement, the sill rule relaxes

Replacing a window in a bedroom that's staying a bedroom is exempt from the strict
sill height requirement, as long as the new window is the largest standard size
that fits the existing opening and opens the same way or wider than the old one.

It still has to open. A picture window still doesn't qualify.

## How to give them the look anyway

This is the useful part, because it turns a no into a sale.

**Pair a picture window with an operable one.** The picture window carries the
view, the operable one carries the code, and side by side most people can't tell
which is which.

**Or use one large casement.** Casements crank wide, so a well sized one can hit
the minimums and still read as clean modern glass.

**Or keep the fixed glass to rooms nobody sleeps in.** Worth thinking about how
that reads from outside first. If most of the house is clean fixed glass and one
bedroom section switches to double hungs, the mismatch can stand out on the
elevation. Sometimes it looks intentional. Sometimes it looks sloppy. If the
bedroom faces the street, it's worth raising.

Room use changes and local requirements change, so confirm with the permit office
before committing a sleeping room to a specific window. The customer facing
version of all this is our post on
[replacing bedroom windows with picture windows](https://www.windowworksnc.com/can-you-replace-bedroom-windows-with-all-picture-windows/).

quiz.q: A customer wants the double hung in their bedroom replaced with a picture window. In which of these bedrooms can you do it?
options: The room has a door out to the patio
The room has another window that opens
The room's only other window is fixed
It's the only window in the room

quiz.q: A bedroom window is large, but the sash only opens a few inches. Does it meet egress?
options: Yes, the glass area is what counts
No, what gets measured is the open hole
Yes, if it's on the ground floor

modules.title: Wall depth and interior finish
modules.body_md:
A window goes in from the outside, and something has to reach the inside face of
the wall. When the window's own jamb doesn't get there, the rest has to be
finished, and there are two ways to do that. **They look completely different and
one is significantly cheaper.**

That makes wall depth a conversation at the appointment rather than a number you
fill in later.

## The wall itself

This part is just construction and it's true of any house, whatever you're
putting in it.

| Total depth | How the wall is built |
|---|---|
| 4-1/2" | 2x4 wall: 3-1/2" stud, 1/2" sheathing, 1/2" drywall |
| 5" or so | 1920s to 30s: 3-1/2" stud, 3/4" plank sheathing, 1" plaster |
| 6-1/2" | 2x6 wall: 5-1/2" stud, 1/2" sheathing, 1/2" drywall |

**A 2x4 wall is 70 to 75% of what you'll see.**

Jamb and extension jamb sizes run about 1/16" deeper than the wall measures,
which is why you'll see 4-9/16" for a 4-1/2" wall. That's deliberate, so the
interior casing folds back toward the wall rather than kicking the other way.

## What each product starts with

This part is manufacturer specific, so it changes depending on what you're
quoting.

**Andersen Tilt Wash and Woodwright are 4-9/16" deep,** which reaches flush on a
2x4. On a 2x6 they don't.

**An Andersen casement jamb is 2-7/8",** so it doesn't reach on anything. This is
why the question comes up on casements far more often.

## Extension jamb sizes available

Also manufacturer specific, and the lists aren't the same.

**Andersen:** 4-9/16", 5-1/4", 6-9/16", 7-1/8". Anything deeper than 7-1/8" has to
be made from scratch.

**Reeb doors:** 4-9/16", 6-9/16", 9-1/4". The 9-1/4" covers very thick walls,
cinder block and similar, and it's rare.

## Option one: extension jambs

The jamb runs all the way to the drywall, then interior casing goes on around it.
Andersen supplies them factory applied in the sizes above.

If the wall is an oddball depth nobody offers, we buy linear lengths of the
largest available size and cut them down on site.

**If you aren't certain of the wall depth, this is the safer route,** because it
can be adjusted to fit.

## Option two: sheetrock returns

Instead of extension jambs, wallboard returns snap into the window to give a flat
surface for the drywall to butt against. The drywall wraps into the opening and
finishes with corner guard. There's no interior casing at all.

Standard on most contemporary homes and common in new construction. It also comes
up in traditional homes when somebody wants a clean look.

**This removes the extension jambs, all the interior mouldings, and the labor to
install them.** On a whole house that can be several thousand dollars.

## On doors

Jamb depth can't be changed in the field. Get it wrong and the door gets
reordered, so it's worth confirming rather than assuming.

modules.title: PO naming
modules.body_md:
Nobody assigns PO numbers. You build one from the customer's name and address,
and the convention is the same every time.

**Last name, street name, street number**, separated by underscores.

So Mr Brown at 1707 Castalia is `Brown_Castalia_1707`.

Street name before street number, which is the opposite of how you'd say the
address out loud. That's deliberate. When somebody is doing several houses on the
same street, this groups them together.

## Phased projects

Add the phase on the end.

`Brown_Castalia_1707_Phase2`

The first phase doesn't get a number. It's only once a second phase exists that
you need to tell them apart.

- Submitting a special order in Reeb
- Quoting Vinyl Design

- The PO column on your commission calculator, which is how a payment gets
  matched back to a job

modules.title: Window anatomy and grille patterns
modules.body_md:
The vocabulary comes up constantly and almost none of it is explained anywhere
else. This is the sheet to come back to.

For doors, our own
[door terminology post](https://www.windowworksnc.com/door-terminology-explained-door-parts-101/)
is a full glossary with a printable, so this sheet covers windows.

## The parts

- **Sash.** The part that holds the glass. A double hung has two, upper and lower
- **Stile.** The vertical pieces of a sash
- **Rail.** The horizontal pieces of a sash
- **Meeting rail**, also called the check rail. Where the two sashes meet on a
  double hung
- **Frame.** The fixed outer structure the sash sits in: two side jambs, the head
  at the top, the sill at the bottom
- **Jamb.** The flat vertical sides of the frame
- **Jamb liner.** The track the sash slides in, running up either side
- **Sill.** The bottom of the frame, sloped outside so water runs off
- **Stool.** The interior shelf at the bottom. What most people mean when they say
  windowsill
- **Casing**, also called moulding. The trim around the outside of the frame,
  inside or out
- **Back band.** A secondary moulding applied around the outer edge of the casing
- **Brickmould.** Exterior trim that finishes the joint between the frame and the
  siding or brick
- **Sill nosing.** The projecting front edge of an exterior sill
- **Balance.** The mechanism in the frame that holds a sash where you put it. When
  a window won't stay up, this has failed
- **Glazing.** Any glass in the window
- **Insulated glass unit**, or IG unit. Two or three panes sealed together with
  argon between them. When this seal fails you get fog between the panes
- **Lite.** One pane of glass, or one section created by a grille
- **Nailing flange**, also called a nailing fin. A thin fin around the frame that
  nails to the sheathing and acts as flashing

## Terms you'll use while quoting

- **Mull.** Joining two or more windows into one unit, so it arrives as a single
  piece rather than separate windows installed side by side
- **Mullion.** The vertical piece between two mulled windows
- **Shim.** A thin wedge used to bring a window plumb, level and square before
  it's fastened
- **Bore.** A pre-drilled hole for a handle set. Single bore is one hole, double
  bore is two
- **Slab.** A door panel on its own, with no frame or hardware
- **Rough opening.** The hole in the wall the window has to fit, before trim
- **Knockdown.** Shipped in pieces to be assembled on site rather than arriving
  built

## How to name a grille pattern

**You count the lites, not the bars.** Upper sash first, then the lower, with
"over" in between.

- **Six over six** is six lites in the upper sash and six in the lower
- **Six over one** is six above and one clear pane below
- **One over one** is no grilles at all

**Some systems count the bars instead.** Two vertical bars and one horizontal bar
gives three columns and two rows, which is six lites. So **2V 1H and six over six
are the same window.** Vinyl Design counts this way and Andersen doesn't, which is
the single easiest thing to get wrong when you're quoting both in one house.

## The patterns

![six over one](quiz-grille-six-over-one.png)
**Six over one.** Six lites above, clear below.

![six over six](quiz-grille-six-over-six.png)
**Six over six.** Six above, six below.

![four over one](quiz-grille-four-over-one.png)
**Four over one.** Four above, clear below.

![four over four](quiz-grille-four-over-four.png)
**Four over four.**

![two by two](quiz-grille-two-by-two.png)
**Two by two.** A single sash divided into four, no upper and lower split.

![equal lite](quiz-grille-equal-lite.png)
**Equal lite.** Horizontal bars only, evenly spaced.

![simulated double hung](quiz-grille-simulated-double-hung.png)
**Simulated double hung.** One horizontal bar across a fixed window, so it reads
as a double hung from outside.

![short fractional](quiz-grille-short-fractional.png)
**Short fractional.** A narrow band of lites across the top.

![nine lite prairie](quiz-grille-nine-lite-prairie.png)
**Nine lite prairie.** Bars set in from the edges, leaving a large open center.
Craftsman and Arts and Crafts homes.

![diamond](quiz-grille-diamond.png)
**Diamond.** Bars at 45 degrees.

## How the grille is built

Three products at very different prices, and they look similar in a photograph.

- **Between the glass**, sometimes GBG. The bars sit inside the sealed unit.
  Nothing to clean around and the flattest looking
- **Simulated divided lite**, or SDL. Bars applied to the inside and outside of
  the glass, often with a spacer between the panes. Reads as a true divided
  window from a few feet away
- **True divided lite**, or TDL. Genuinely separate panes held by real muntins.
  The most authentic and the most expensive
- **Removable interior.** Clips onto the inside of the sash and can be taken off.
  Not available on every line

**Muntin** is the traditional word for a grille bar, from when they held separate
panes rather than dividing one.

modules.title: The Value Match Guarantee
modules.body_md:
## Say the whole thing

**Never say "price match."**

Price match invites a bare number comparison, which is exactly what the terms
exist to prevent. Say **Value Match Guarantee**, every time, because we match
what they get, not just what they pay. Getting the words right in front of a
customer matters. It's the difference between a promise we can keep and one we
can't.

## The promise

> Buy from Window Works Co. with complete confidence. If within 30 days of
> signing you show us a written, detailed quote from another licensed, insured
> contractor for the same windows, the same installation, and the same warranty
> at a lower total price, we'll refund you the difference and give you an
> extra $100.
>
> **You'll never overpay buying from us.**

## Why it holds up

The refund only fires when a licensed local competitor commits **in writing**
to the identical product, the same installation method, the same air sealing
and materials, and the same warranty, at a lower total, and will confirm it on
a phone call.

A lowball quote or a big box store almost never matches all of that on paper.
The cheap version skimps on exactly the things that don't show up in a photo:
little or no foam, builder grade caulk, a shorter labor warranty. Line the two
up honestly and they stop being comparable.

**It has never been paid out.** Not because the terms are a trap, but because
the quotes don't line up. Big box labor warranties run one year against our two.
Most contractors don't carry the insurance we do, which matters to a homeowner
the day somebody gets hurt on their property.

If a competitor ever does beat all of it, we'd be glad to pay the $100 to find
out who they are.

## The eight conditions

**1. Equivalent product.** Identical manufacturer, product line, series, frame
material, glass package, hardware, and interior and exterior color. Grilles
must match in construction, pattern, and bar specification. GBG (grilles between
the glass), simulated divided lite, and true divided lite are different products
at very different prices, so the same pattern built as a cheaper grille type
doesn't qualify.

**2. Equivalent installation.** Full frame to full frame, or pocket and insert
to pocket and insert.

With a comparable air sealing package: minimal expansion polyurethane foam
formulated for windows and doors around the full perimeter, since standard
expanding foam bows the frame and doesn't qualify, and a premium exterior grade
sealant pressed into a cleaned joint rather than laid over the top of it.

Plus flashing integration appropriate to the installation type, interior and
exterior trim where it's a full frame job, and debris haul away.

Builder grade acrylic caulk, unfoamed gaps, or a stripped down job isn't
equivalent.

**3. Equivalent warranty.** Same or better labor warranty term. Product warranty
comes with the product, so if it's genuinely the same product that part matches
by default. **Ours is two years on workmanship,** so a competitor at
one year doesn't qualify.

**4. Same job.** Same opening count, same measured sizes and options.

**5. Licensed and insured competitor.** Licensed in North Carolina, insured for
this work, serving the area where the home is.

**6. Written and scope specific.** Signed and dated, stating the product and the
full scope with a total package price, from a contractor we can call. No line item
breakdown required, since we compare on total. Details a quote wouldn't
normally list, like the specific foam or sealant, we confirm on our verification
call. Verbal quotes, texts, screenshots, and ballpark ranges don't qualify.

**7. Current timing.** Shown to us within 30 days of signing, and the quote
must state its validity period, which must still be in effect.

**8. Total to total.** We compare **the final price after every discount has
come off, including ours.** Not the subtotal before discounts, and not the
product on its own without adders.

The three day deal, the authorized discount, the cash discount, and the referral
bonus all come off before we compare. That works in our favor. The lower our
final number, the harder it is for anyone to beat it.

## Never eligible

Clearance, floor models, discontinued, liquidation, going out of business, or
employee and friends and family pricing.

Quotes containing errors or omissions, or that the issuing contractor won't
honor or verify.

Labor only or product only quotes.

Anything submitted more than 30 days after signing.

Any quote we can't verify directly with the contractor who issued it.

## The claim process

The customer submits the written competing quote within 30 days of signing.

We verify it directly with the issuing contractor, to confirm it's real,
current, and equivalent, and to resolve any suspected error with them.

At our option we either match the price plus $100, or decline with a written
explanation of the differences.

One claim per contract, available only to the named customer, not transferable.

## Running it at the table

**It's an objection remover, not a discount.** Lead with it to close today.
Never use it to justify dropping your price.

When a customer raises a cheaper number:

**There's no need to move on price.** The guarantee is exactly why they
can buy today with zero risk.

**Ask for the written, detailed quote.** This alone ends most price objections,
because the comparison rarely exists on paper.

**Look it over.** You know what our quote includes, so you'll often spot right
away where theirs is lighter. A one year labor warranty. No mention of
foam or sealant. Capping instead of replacing the trim. Point those out and help
the customer understand what the difference actually is.

**If it isn't obvious, or if it looks genuinely equivalent, it goes to the COO.**
You don't make that call at the table. It's eight conditions with a lot of
detail in them, and it's his to evaluate.

**Where the gap is product, we can re-spec.** If their number is lower because of
color, grille type, glass package, or screens, we can quote our installation with
those choices instead, so the customer sees the real trade and makes it
themselves. Most decline once they see what they give up.

**Where the gap is labor, we can't.** There's no cheaper version of our
installation. If their price is lower because they're capping, skipping the
foam, or running a one year warranty, that isn't a lesser version of our quote.
It's a different job.

modules.title: Presenting in Ingage
modules.body_md:
Ingage is the presentation app on your iPad. It's what you walk a customer
through at the table, and it's the same deck every time.

The software itself is simple. Four things are worth knowing before you use it in
front of somebody.

## Open it before the appointment starts

If you've already tapped into the presentation once, it opens right away when
you need it. That way you and the homeowners aren't waiting around while it
loads.

## Use the blue icon, not the black one

The Demo tile shows two things that look like the Ingage presentation.

The **blue** one is what you present from. The **black** one with the suitcase
exists only so Vendo can email the customer a link at the end.

## Downloaded content works offline, links don't

The deck itself presents fine without WiFi. Web link buttons and HTML pages won't
load, so if you're somewhere with no signal, those are the parts that break.

**The reviews link under Satisfied Customers is one of them.** Worth knowing
before you build up to it in a house with no service.

## What's in it

Seven sections, in this order.

- **About us.** Founded 2007, ten thousand customers, family owned. Our three
  guiding principles, and proof of insurance and licensing. **Satisfied
  Customers** opens a page that links out to our reviews
- **Cost vs. value.** The Zonda Cost vs. Value report, which is independent data
  on what window replacement returns at resale
- **Products and services.** Entry doors, and windows and patio doors
- **Installation process.** Justin on video explaining how we install, then a
  slide with popups on the three things that make a top tier install: no
  capping, correct sealing, and a correct expansion joint
- **Gallery.** Windows, doors, before and afters, and sunroom conversions
- **Our guarantee.** The two year workmanship warranty, and the Value Match
  Guarantee
- **Review.** A recap of why us, and the financing options

## Getting around it

**Anything blinking can be tapped**, and it opens a popup with more detail on it.

You can move through the deck by tabbing along the bottom, or by scrolling.

**It isn't built to be presented front to back.** It's designed so you can go
straight to the section a particular customer cares about. What they want to talk
about decides the order, not the deck.

**We build this deck in house.** If you're presenting it and something would land
better in a different order, or a slide is missing something customers keep
asking about, tell the Technology Officer. It changes when somebody says so.

## It sits on the table

The deck is built 4:3 for an iPad, and it's meant to face the customer on a
counter or a table rather than be held like a clipboard.

## Practising it

You'll get ninety minutes to run the presentation on your own, and then you'll
deliver it to the Technology Officer as though she's a customer. Both of those
are their own items later in the path.

modules.title: Taking great pictures in CompanyCam
modules.body_md:
Your photos get used four ways.

**Project management and installation** need to know what they're walking into.
Damage, rot, access, anything unusual, and what the site itself is like to work
on.

**Marketing** uses the exteriors. They can take their own in progress and after
photos, but the before shot can only come from whoever was at the initial
consultation.

**You** need them more than you expect. Was that a 445 or a 442? What was the
grille pattern? What hardware finish am I matching on the second phase of this
job? A photo answers it in seconds.

**And they protect us.** If a homeowner says our crew damaged something, what the
house looked like before we arrived is the answer.

## Settings

Two to set before you start.

**Timestamp on.** A photo without a date is much weaker as a record.

**Latitude and longitude off.** We don't want customer addresses sitting in photo
metadata, particularly on anything that ends up in marketing.

## Document what was already there

Photograph any damage you find, **including things that have nothing to do with
windows or doors.** Holes in drywall, cracks in a driveway, a chipped tile, a
dented gutter, a scuffed floor.

Most damage claims come from a homeowner noticing something they had never looked
at closely before. A dated photo taken before our crew was ever on site settles
it in one message.

## Exteriors

**Level.** CompanyCam has a level tool for this.

**Landscape, not portrait.** Portrait makes sense for a single window or door.
An exterior needs the width.

**The front of the home, with as many of its angles as will fit in frame.** Roof
edges, the peak, the chimney, both sides. Don't cut off the top of the roof.
Backing up too far is fine, we can crop it down afterwards. Losing the peak we
can't fix.

One wide shot does something a set of close ups can't. **The project manager is
looking at the whole setup**: how steep the driveway is, where a ladder can
safely go, what's in the way. None of that shows up in individual window shots,
and it's the difference between planning the install from your photos and having
to go out and look.

**All four elevations** where you can get them safely.

**Watch for your own reflection in the glass.** Move a few feet if you can see
yourself in a window.

**Never take a photo with a child in the frame.**

**Keep identifying information out of frame** where you can, license plates
mostly. Those can come out in Photoshop, but it's less work for everyone if they
were never in the shot.

## Interiors

**Ask before you turn on lights.** Then turn them back off when you're done.
Without interior light you get a silhouette against a bright window and the
photo is useless.

**Capture the entire framing** around each window and door, not just the
opening. Moulding, casing, hardware, all of it in one shot.

**Document any damage.** Rot especially. If you suspect water damage in a wall
below a window, photograph it and say so. That's exactly the heads up the PM
and crew need before they arrive.

## Details worth shooting

- **Moulding profiles**
- **Hardware colors**
- **Grille patterns**, particularly anything unusual. A nine over one isn't
  common and you won't remember it
- **Architectural oddities** like a bump out, which tells the install team what
  they're dealing with

## Do your best

Terrain, weather, pets, parked cars, drapes, safety, and the occasional palm
tree directly in front of the door all get in the way. Sometimes you can't get
the shot, and that's understood. Get what you can.

modules.title: 100 Series single and double hung
modules.body_md:
The 100 Series is Andersen's entry level line and an extremely popular one. It's
all Fibrex fiberglass composite, with no wood anywhere, inside or out.

There are two hung windows in the line and they're very different products.

## The single hung

Only the bottom sash operates. The top is fixed. It doesn't tilt in.

It's a side load, meaning you pull clips and pop the sash out, and that is
designed for service and sash replacement rather than cleaning. It isn't a
simple job.

There's noticeable play in the sash when you move it, which reads worse than the
window actually is. That's a design characteristic rather than a quality problem,
and it's why this has never been a favorite of ours.

## The double hung

Recently released and the opposite story. Both sashes operate, it tilts in for
cleaning, there's no play in the sash, and the frame is solid.

**This is the one to sell.** We expect it to become one of our top sellers over
the next decade, and it's our answer whenever someone is shopping vinyl
replacement, especially if they want black on the outside.

The field it competes in is Renewal by Andersen, Marvin Infinity, Pella, and
ProVia, all of which sit at the higher end of fiberglass.

## What Fibrex gives you

It doesn't rot. It's made from recycled sawdust and wood bound with polymer resin
from fiberglass, so it's a genuinely green product, and it's **2.5 times stronger
than vinyl.**

The color is integral to the material rather than painted on top. Scratch a
painted vinyl window and you find a different color underneath. Scratch this and
you have to go a long way in before you reach anything different.

## Sizing and options

It uses **nominal sizing**, which the [Sizing conventions](module:REF-030) sheet
explains. That suits replacing existing vinyl from new construction. It also
customizes in eighth inch increments, so it's forgiving and cost effective.

**Exterior colors** are white, Sandtone, Terratone, dark bronze, and black, and
two tone is available.

**Grilles** are SDL or between the glass. Removable grilles aren't available on
any 100 Series window.

**Hardware** is always the metal slimline lock, which the
[Never sell, always include](module:REF-040) sheet covers.

modules.title: 100 Series casement and awning
modules.body_md:
Casements and awnings are both crank operated, so they're covered together here.

**Casements** crank out to the right or the left. **Awnings** crank upward, and
only about 30 degrees rather than 90, which is worth saying out loud to a
homeowner who's picturing full ventilation.

Either one can be ordered stationary, meaning it looks the same but doesn't open.

**A stationary unit can never provide egress,** and it looks identical to an
operable one from outside. The [Egress and sleeping rooms](module:REF-060) sheet
covers what to check before you put one in a room somebody sleeps in.

## Stationary casement or awning, versus a picture window

If you have several units in a row and some don't open, a stationary casement
or awning keeps the visible sash line so the whole row looks uniform from
outside. Nobody can tell which ones operate.

A picture window has no sash. The frame runs across in one piece.

Picture is less expensive, and above certain sizes casement isn't available so
picture is the only option. Below that, it's a look decision.

## The casement conversion

This is a real sales play. A customer with a bank of old wood double hungs can
go back with 100 Series casements as inserts and completely change the look of
the house at a reasonable price.

The 100 Series is the line for this, because its eighth inch custom sizing is
cheap and forgiving. On the 400 Series the same conversion costs considerably
more.

## Details

These share the Fibrex, the glass packages, and the colors with the rest of the
100 Series.

**Screens** come in fiberglass mesh, which is the less expensive option, or
TruScene. A casement only ever takes a full screen.

**Locks** differ between the two. An awning gets one on each side. A casement
gets a single lock in the lower corner, with folding hardware.

modules.title: 100 Series gliding windows
modules.body_md:
**If you're selling a gliding window at Window Works, this is almost certainly
the one.** Across every brand and every line we carry, it's the one we reach for.

One panel slides and the other is fixed, and you choose the operating side
**viewed from the exterior.** Unlike a double casement, you can't open both.

## Why it wins

Fibrex lets it go bigger than vinyl. A double reaches six by six, and triples run
to roughly twelve feet.

Triples come symmetrical, or uneven with a fixed picture center and gliding
ends.

**Screened porch conversions are where we sell the most of them.** Those
openings are whatever someone framed years ago, with no standard sizing, and
this window customizes to fit. Pair it with 100 Series casements and picture
windows to fill a whole run.

The real advantage on a porch is space. Casements crank out into wherever people
are walking or sitting. Gliders don't take any space at all, so a patio, a set
of stairs, or a table and chairs stays usable.

Also works as a pass through from a kitchen to a porch or patio, at a fraction
of what a multi glide or bifold would cost.

Available without a nailing flange, so it can go in as an insert where a
picture window was, or where two double hungs come out and the divider between
them goes with them.

## Easy Breeze

The competitor you'll meet on porch conversions. Local contractors and
dealers push it hard in the Triangle.

It's a vinyl triple track system, and the panel is vinyl rather than glass. It's
plastic, and you can press on it with your hand.

For a four season room where the customer wants real heating and cooling
performance, it isn't a comparable product.

## Hardware

Always the slimline metal lock, at about five to ten dollars a window. We don't
present it as a choice, we just include it, because the plastic one breaks.

modules.title: 100 Series gliding door
modules.body_md:
This is our budget gliding patio door, and a good one.

It's Fibrex, so it doesn't rot, and it's priced right around vinyl and sometimes
under ProVia. Well below the 200, 400, E and A Series.

## Fibrex versus vinyl, and this is where it matters most

**Fibrex is 2.5 times stronger than vinyl.** If you're going to make that
comparison anywhere, make it here.

Vinyl gliding doors get problematic over time. The glass panels are heavy and
plastic framing struggles to carry that weight, so you get warping and
operation problems as the panel presses into the frame. Fibrex carries it.

Be fair about the exception: ProVia puts steel reinforcing in their door
panels, which helps a great deal. Not all vinyl is equal, and saying so makes
you more credible, not less.

The cheap gliding doors at a big box store are a different matter. That is
where the real problems come from.

## What it is and isn't

**Two panel only.** There's no four panel option in the 100 Series.

One panel operates and the other is fixed. **Choose the operating side viewed
from the exterior.**

**It can't be ordered knockdown.** The frame is integrally built and doesn't screw
together in the field, which is the opposite of the 400 Series.

## Details

**Sizes** start at about five feet and run up to eight feet tall, with six feet
being standard, and they customize.

**Hardware is limited to two handle sets,** both metal. Tulsa comes in white,
Sandtone, or black. Afton covers satin nickel, bright brass, antique brass, and
black.

**The auxiliary foot lock is always included**, at about fifteen dollars. It's a
slightly different design from the 400 Series version but does the same job.

**Screens** are fiberglass mesh only, on a standard sliding screen panel.
TruScene isn't available on any door because it's considered a hazard.

Glass options are the same as the rest of the line.

modules.title: 100 Series picture and specialty
modules.body_md:
Picture windows are most of what you'll sell out of this part of the line.
Specialty shapes are available too, but limited.

## The frame rule, and it applies to the whole 100 Series

**The frame is 3-1/4 inches per side.** That means 6-1/2 inches of any unit
dimension is frame, in both directions.

A 12 by 12 picture window leaves you 5-1/2 inches of glass. It doesn't look
good.

We've had this go wrong. A customer was told, went ahead anyway, saw the window at
pickup and wanted to return it. Once it's ordered, we own it and so do they.

So on anything small, a walk in closet or a short wide unit, look at a specialty
window instead. The rule holds across the gliders, the single hung and the
casements too, and the smaller the unit, the more pronounced the frame.

## Where picture windows work

Big sizes are where they're excellent. They run up to six by eight because Fibrex
carries the weight, and down to one by one, customizable in eighth inch
increments.

**Screened porch conversions**, where they fill openings alongside the gliding
windows.

**Living rooms** where a customer has a bank of old wood double hungs and tells
you they never open them anyway. Converting those to energy efficient picture
windows is a nicer look, and we've done plenty of them.

**Sleeping rooms need an egress check first.** A picture window is fixed, so its
clear opening is zero and it can never satisfy egress on its own. That doesn't
rule it out, but it does mean something else in the room has to provide the way
out.

The [Egress and sleeping rooms](module:REF-060) sheet has the rules, the North
Carolina numbers, and the three ways to give a customer the look anyway.

## What it looks like

There's no sash, so the frame runs across in one piece. Compare that with a
stationary casement or awning, which keeps the sash line. In a row of units, that
difference shows.

No welded sash corner either, so you get a clean miter with none of the rough
edges you see on a vinyl window.

## Specialty shapes

Trapezoids, half circles, and so on are available in the 100 Series, but the
thick frame works against them. Small sizes lose most of their glass, and
lining up angles for a roofline is harder with a heavy profile.

For most architectural shapes, Andersen specialty or E-Series is the better
answer. The 100 Series is less expensive, but more limited, and it won't look as
good.

modules.title: 400 Series Tilt Wash double hung
modules.body_md:
One of two double hungs in the 400 Series. The other is the Woodwright, and
they're different windows. **Always say Tilt Wash or Woodwright, never "400
Series double hung."** The shared name confuses customers, contractors, and
everyone else.

This is Andersen's workhorse, sitting above their lower lines and below the upper
ones. It's one of our top sellers as a full frame application, and it's easy to
service because it comes apart and back together cleanly.

## Construction

It's a wood frame with a wood interior in unfinished pine, vinyl clad on both the
frame and the sashes. The sill is Fibrex composite with a 14 degree pitch, which
is the standard pitch for old wood windows.

## Why it sells

**Stock sizes match traditional wood window sizes.** Full frame tear out to the
studs and no customization needed.

That keeps the continuity of the home's look, limits siding and exterior work,
and if you go back with the same size moulding inside you usually avoid paint
lines. Not guaranteed, and it isn't in our labor contract, but usually.

Both sashes tilt in, though it's harder than on the upper lines because there's no tilt latch built into the lock.

## Config traps

**Custom sizing exists in eighth inch increments and will price you out of the
deal.** On an old wood window you almost certainly don't need it.

**Black or dark bronze interiors are only available matching the same
exterior.** Black outside allows black or white inside. Dark bronze allows dark
bronze or white. White outside with black inside isn't available on this
window, though Andersen allows it on other lines.

**There's no factory stain.** It comes as unfinished pine, and staining it
afterwards is somebody else's job. We don't offer staining.

## Never sell

**Optional lift hardware.** Andersen moved framing up for energy performance
and it no longer lines up, sitting above the glass. They still sell it. We sold
expensive bright brass hand lifts to a customer who chose the window for them
and then couldn't fit them. Fine on the Woodwright, never here.

## Details

**Hardware** comes two ways, both metal. The standard locking keeper is white,
stone, or black. The Estate locking keeper covers antique brass, bright brass,
distressed bronze, and satin nickel, and it comes up most in kitchens where
somebody is matching cabinet hardware.

**Exterior colors** run to seven. White is 75 to 80 percent of what you'll sell
and black is second. Terratone and forest green show up in wooded and rural
settings.

**Trim** from Andersen is Fibrex, and it's nice when it works, but the spacing
fails in brick openings. We use PVC brickmould instead, and white PVC matches
Andersen white closely enough that most people don't paint it.

**The product ID** is `TW` followed by the sash size, so `TW2636` is 2 feet 6 by
3 feet 6.

modules.title: 400 Series Woodwright double hung
modules.body_md:
This is the other 400 Series double hung, and it's a step above the Tilt Wash.

## Why they share a name

When both launched the frame was essentially the same: same PVC wrap on the
upper frame, same Fibrex sill, both sized to replace old wood windows. They
have diverged since, and the sashes were always different.

Which is why you never say "400 Series double hung" to anybody.

## What makes it the upgrade

**The sash is architecturally correct.** Go into a colonial home, or anywhere in
New England, and the old wood sashes look like this one.

**There's more wood in it.** The jamb liners are wood where the Tilt Wash uses
PVC, which is where the name comes from.

**The sash exterior is all Fibrex** rather than vinyl clad, which gives it a more
beveled, cleaner profile.

**The tilt release is easy.** The mechanism is built into the lock, so you unlock
it, keep turning, and the lower sash disengages. The top sash has tilt pins.

**You get wood species options,** which are unfinished pine, maple, or oak.
There's still no factory stain.

## Same as the Tilt Wash

It uses the same sash sizing, so the same full frame pitch applies: tear out to
the studs, no customizing needed, the look stays continuous, and siding and
interior work are limited. Paint lines still aren't guaranteed.

Exterior colors, glass options, and trim limitations are all the same too, so
it's PVC brickmould again.

## Different from the Tilt Wash

**Hand lifts work fine here**, so sell them if a customer wants them. This is the
opposite of the Tilt Wash rule.

**There's no estate hardware**, which was discontinued long ago. Easy tilt release
is the only style, though you can still pick finishes. If a customer has old
Woodwright windows and wants to match the original hardware, that can be special
quoted.

## Product ID

The product ID is `WDH` plus the sash size, so `WDH3442` is 3 feet 4 by 4 feet 2.
Unit dimensions run larger because of the frame.

One measuring note: stated height runs from the top of the frame to the very
bottom of the sloped sill, so the interior sits a little higher than the number
suggests.

modules.title: 400 Series casement
modules.body_md:
There's one casement in the 400 Series. Unlike the double hungs, there are no
variants to keep straight.

It cranks out to the right or the left, and it can be ordered stationary, which
comes up on a three panel where the center doesn't open.

**A stationary casement can never provide egress,** and it looks identical to an
operable one from outside. The [Egress and sleeping rooms](module:REF-060) sheet
covers what to check before you put one in a room somebody sleeps in.

## Construction

It's vinyl clad over a pine frame, wrapped 360 degrees including the sash, with the
wood sealed inside the vinyl. So it doesn't rot, and it has the strength and
rigidity of real wood behind it.

Painted interiors use a baked on polyurethane rubber base paint, so there are no
brushstrokes. That holds across the painted Andersen line.

## Finishing the inside

**A casement jamb is 2-7/8" deep,** so it never reaches the inside face of the
wall. Tilt Wash and Woodwright are 4-9/16" and reach flush on a 2x4, which is why
this comes up on casements far more often.

The remaining depth gets finished with either extension jambs or sheetrock
returns. Those look completely different and one costs a lot less, so it's worth
raising at the appointment. The
[Wall depth and interior finish](module:REF-070) sheet covers both, with the
standard depths.

## Sizing

Casements don't match old wood double hung openings, so a full frame conversion
almost always means customizing. Stock sizing does exist and is worth checking
anyway, because occasionally you get lucky.

Custom costs more, the same as it does on the double hungs.

## The kitchen sink play

Even in a house full of double hungs, people often want one casement behind the
sink. Cranking beats reaching across the counter to lift a sash.

Pair it with estate hardware matching their cabinet finishes and you have a
specific, high value recommendation you can make in almost every kitchen.

**Check where the crank lands before you order.** A casement cranks from one side,
and if that side is the faucet side, the crank and the faucet can end up in the
same place. We've had them line up exactly, which meant the window couldn't go in
and had to be reordered.

So look at the sink, look at the faucet, and pick the operating side that puts the
crank clear of it.

## Details

**Grilles** come up less often here. It's one sheet of glass and most people want
the view.

**Exterior colors** are the same seven as the rest of the 400. White leads, but
black is climbing on casements, particularly on contemporary homes or a house
doing casements throughout.

**Traditional versus contemporary** differs only in the interior glass stops. It's
hard to see on the website and clearer in the quoting schematic.

**The product ID** starts with `C`. The numbers after it are Andersen's own
designation with no sash or nominal logic behind them, so there's nothing to
decode.

modules.title: 400 Series awning
modules.body_md:
This is Andersen's best selling awning, though we don't sell many of them in this
market.

It's vinyl clad over a wood frame with a wood interior, and it has a slim profile
that suits contemporary homes.

## The 30 degree fact

**An awning cranks up about 30 degrees, not 90.**

So the ventilation is more limited than a casement of the same size, and it's
worth saying at the table rather than after it's installed.

## Frame depth

**The frame is 2-1/8" deep,** which is even shallower than the casement, so the
inside has to be finished with extension jambs or sheetrock returns on any wall.

Across the 400 Series, the double hungs reach the interior on a 2x4 and the
casements and awnings don't. The
[Wall depth and interior finish](module:REF-070) sheet covers both options.

## Sizes don't combine freely

Seeing a width range of 35-15/16" to 71-7/8" doesn't mean you can pair the widest
width with any height in the height range. The crank up geometry rules out certain
combinations.

So check the allowable configurations in Vendo before you promise a size.

## Profile consistency

If a house mixes awnings and casements, keep the profile consistent across all of
them, either contemporary or traditional throughout. The two share a profile
family, so mixing them looks wrong.

## Details

**Interior colors are limited by the exterior,** the same as on the Tilt Wash.
Black outside allows black or white inside, dark bronze allows dark bronze or
white, and white outside with black inside isn't available.

**Wood** comes as unfinished pine or prefinished white. There are no species
upgrades and no factory stain.

**Hardware matches the casements.** Contemporary folding is standard in white,
stone, or black, with bright brass, distressed bronze, satin nickel, and oil
rubbed bronze as upgrades. Oil rubbed bronze is usually written and spoken as ORB.

**The product ID** starts with `A`, and the numbers after it don't decode.

modules.title: 400 Series picture windows
modules.body_md:
A picture window doesn't open. They're usually square, sometimes rectangular, and
often large.

**A sleeping room needs an egress check before you quote one.** A fixed window has
a clear opening of zero, so it can't provide the way out on its own. The
[Egress and sleeping rooms](module:REF-060) sheet has the rules and the ways to
give a customer the look anyway.

## There are three of them

Andersen's website doesn't tell you there are three, and the difference only shows
up once you're configuring the window in Vendo.

The 400 Series has a picture window profile for each partner line:

- One to match the **Tilt Wash**, with a sloped sill and a vinyl clad surround
- One to match the **Woodwright**, sloped sill and Fibrex surround
- One to match the **casement and awning**, which share a profile

Match the picture window to the line the customer chose. The wrong profile in a row
of Tilt Wash shows up on the elevation.

## Sizing

**Picture windows don't follow traditional wood window sizes.** Replacing an
old wood picture window means customizing, every time.

Within the 400 Series the double hungs match traditional wood sizes and the
casements and picture windows don't, so don't generalize from one product to the
next.

## Details

Interior and exterior colors, grille patterns, trim options, and glass are all the
same as the rest of the 400.

**The product ID** starts with `P`. A contemporary `P3535` is the casement and
awning profile.

modules.title: 400 Series specialty windows
modules.body_md:
This one is about knowing what's possible rather than knowing the detail.

Andersen makes a very wide range of shapes: ovals, circles, trapezoids, arches,
eyebrows which are short arches, and triangles including right and isosceles. They
come as single units or configured as multiple staged windows.

They're available across essentially all Andersen's lines, some better suited than
others.

**These are fixed, so none of them can provide egress.** The
[Egress and sleeping rooms](module:REF-060) sheet covers what to check before you
put one in a room somebody sleeps in.

## Specialty isn't only fancy shapes

The specialty division also handles custom sized square and rectangular picture
windows, and transoms above a window, in sizes the regular lines won't build.

That's worth holding on to. Specialty sounds exotic, and most of the time it just
means a size the standard catalog can't do.

## What a rep should take from this

Walking into a house and seeing an odd window isn't an automatic no. Andersen
probably makes it, or can create it, usually as a custom or special order.

You likely won't be able to price it on the spot, and that's fine. Recognize what
it is, tell the customer we can almost certainly do it, and hand it to the COO.

## Design rule

On anything angled, follow the roof line. That isn't a matter of taste, it just
looks wrong when it doesn't.

modules.title: 400 Series patio doors, hinged and gliding
modules.body_md:
The 400 Series has a hinged patio door and a gliding one, and they're covered
together here.

## Andersen undersizes doors

**Their 6'8" is 79.5". Doors in the field are around 82".**

For a standard 6'8" opening you need the **6'11" option, 82-3/8"**.

It's a measuring convention. Other door companies quote the panel and add the
frame separately. Andersen gives you the whole product including the frame, so
selecting 6'8" because the existing door is a 6'8" gets you something that won't
fit.

## Hinged, the French wood door

It comes double or single, full lite, with a traditional profile and more wood
around the glass.

**The multi-point lock is the best in the industry.** Deadbolt locks the entire
handle set so you can't lift or push the handle. And Andersen builds the
active and passive panel activation into the hardware, so there's no astragal
with flip levers to fumble with. Push either handle and both panels operate.

Worth contrasting with Therma-Tru, whose multi-point we won't sell because
it fails. Andersen builds in house. Therma-Tru ships to distributors who
assemble. Same feature, opposite verdict, and that contrast explains our whole
brand position.

The 400 Series hinged door is frozen in time. The A-Series looks nearly
identical with far more options. This one still works well, but colors and
options are limited.

**The hinges adjust,** so you can raise, lower, or shift the panel. That matters
here because our clay soil never stops moving houses, so a door that goes out of
reveal can be brought back rather than replaced.

## Gliding, the French wood glider

This one has traditional thick lower panels on a ball bearing roller track.

**Raised track, almost like a monorail,** so dirt and debris fall away instead
of jamming the rollers the way recessed tracks used to.

**The rollers adjust with a Phillips head** from the inside, for the same reason
the hinges do.

200 and 400 Series gliders share the same frame, rollers, and hardware. Only
the panel profile differs.

Standard width is 71.25", and gliders go much larger than hinged doors because the
support system is different. They run up to what Andersen calls 8 foot, which is
an actual unit of 95-1/4", and 8 foot in height.

The handle is a C handle, which is standard across most brands.

## Two rules

**Order knockdown, always.** Safer to handle, less damage, one person can
deliver it, and there's a small price break. Our crews assemble in 15 to 20
minutes. We don't offer assembled. Note the 100 Series glider can't be
ordered this way.

**Include the auxiliary foot lock, always, without asking.** Thirty to
thirty five dollars. A real deadbolt shoot bolt operated with your foot, and it
can be drilled for a second position so the door locks while vented.

## Hardware finishes are style specific

There isn't a universal palette, so the finish depends on which style you pick.

- **Albany** is white, black, or stone only
- **Tribeca** is white or stone
- **Anvers** gets satin nickel, bright brass, or ORB
- **FSB** is stainless only
- **Ashley Norton** has the widest range

The names correspond across hinged and gliding, and every style and every finish
is a different price.

## Blinds between the glass

These are available on stock sizes and lost if you customize. They're excellent
for kids and pets because they can't be damaged, and they never need cleaning
because they're sealed in.

## Pro tip that applies everywhere

The website and the quoting software disagree, and neither is reliably current.
**Go with what Vendo will let you build.**

## Product IDs

`FWG` is the French wood glider. `FWI` is in swing hinged and `FWO` is out swing.
Out swing is discontinued but still shows on the website.
