modules.title: Quoting Therma-Tru doors in Reeb 2G
modules.body_md:
Reeb is the distributor we buy Therma-Tru doors from, and Reeb 2G is their
quoting software. Keep it on your iPad home screen.

## How Therma-Tru actually works, and why it matters

Therma-Tru manufactures fiberglass door panels and door slabs and ships them to
distributors around the country. **The distributor assembles the door in the
frame and hangs it, in their own shop.** They also do the prefinishing.

So quality varies by distributor. Reeb is good, and does a nice job on
prefinishes. Others in the area over the years haven't been.

Contrast that with Andersen and ProVia, who build everything in house and ship
on their own logistics.

Most people assume a Therma-Tru door is built by Therma-Tru, whether they buy
it from us or a big box store. It's not. Worth understanding, because it is
also why we don't sell their multi-point lock.

## Getting around

Use Projects to reopen an existing quote, or start a new one and hit Go.

Reeb carries a lot of building supply products, and **we generally sell only their
Therma-Tru doors.** The exception is residential fire doors, if somebody needs a 20
minute fire rated door from the house to the garage.

Exterior Doors is the section you want.

## Choosing a line

Classic Craft, Fiber Classic, and Smooth Star all have a composite edge, with
no wood exposed to the elements. **Those are the three.**

Reeb also offers wood doors and their own economy fiberglass. Neither is one we
sell, and the never list below says why.

## Everything is viewed from the exterior

This matters most on configuration, and especially on sidelights.

Standing outside, the sidelight on the right is a right sidelight. Pick it from
the inside and the customer gets a door with the sidelight on the wrong side.

So even when you're standing inside the house working it out, it's the opposite of
what you're looking at.

## Working through the build

First entry versus hinged patio versus fixed, then the configuration: single,
single with sidelights, transoms, or double.

**Widths are the slab, not the finished unit.** A 28, 30, or 34 is the door panel
and you still have to account for the frame. Heights are usually 6'8" or 8'0".

Then panel style, flat or raised, the glass options, grille patterns, and whether
the SDL is composite or aluminum.

**Colors.** Reeb's own palette, Therma-Tru Prismaguard, or Sherwin Williams
color match. Sherwin Williams costs more, but it removes all the back and
forth. You just need the color number. And if a customer is torn between two
colors, pick one to close the deal. Pricing is identical and we can edit it
later.

Exterior and interior are separate, so two tone is easy.

**Handing.** In swing or out swing, left or right. Match the existing swing
unless they specifically want a change. Ninety plus percent do not. But when a
door swings into a tight space, changing it can transform the room, and that is
worth raising.

**Brickmould** is standard or flat casing, so check what they already have. Always
Frame Saver. Shipped loose is usually no, occasionally yes on brick or rock work so
the installers can adjust.

**Hinges** are standard radius by square almost always. Ball bearing, self
closing, and adjustable are upgrades.

**Jamb depth** is 4-9/16" for a 2x4, 6-9/16" for a 2x6, and 9-1/4" for very thick
walls. **It can't be changed in the field,** so getting it wrong means the door is
reordered. The [Wall depth and interior finish](module:REF-070) sheet covers how
the walls are built.

**The sill** is composite adjustable, always. Sill horns are rare, and a bronze
finish only comes with a dark cap.

**The accessible option** shows up in Reeb as adaptive ADA, or public access with
thermal break. You'll hear people in the industry just call it an ADA sill, and
that's fine.

It's worth raising more often than you'd think. It sits lower and flatter, it's far
easier to cross, and the standard composite sill is a trip hazard for some people
even when it drops.

Who it's for is broader than a wheelchair. Anyone with a chronic condition or
mobility challenge, older customers who want to age in place, younger ones pushing
a stroller through the door every day, and anyone who hosts a visitor who'd
struggle with a standard sill.

**The ADA itself only applies to businesses,** so a homeowner isn't required to meet
it. What they usually want is a door that works for them rather than one that
satisfies a standard.

If a customer does ask about the guidelines, our post on
[ADA compliant doors](https://www.windowworksnc.com/an-in-depth-guide-to-getting-an-ada-compliant-door-for-your-home/)
covers them, including the 32" clear opening and the lever handle rather than a
round knob.

This is a real conversation about making their home work for them, not an upsell.

**Locks.** Use an entry lock, single or double bore, with a 2-3/8" back set, which
is what most hardware at Lowe's or Home Depot fits. Say yes to strike jamb prep,
Schlage Baldwin standard.

**Weather stripping** to suit the door color.

**Accessories.** All of these are upcharges and all of them are optional.

**Kick plate.** Rare, but worth asking about if their existing door has one. It also
does real work on a house with young kids or a stroller going through the door
every day.

**Peephole.** Rare now, mostly because of Ring cameras, but sell it if they want
it. Match the finish to the hardware they're choosing.

**Mail slot.** Also an option, also rare.

**Where peepholes and mail slots do come up** is older Raleigh neighborhoods, Five
Points and similar, where somebody is upgrading efficiency and looks while keeping
the character of the house. Both are part of that character, and losing them can be
the thing a customer notices afterwards. Worth asking rather than assuming.

**Sill cover is always yes,** a couple of dollars, and it protects the door in
transit.

## Never on a Reeb door

Five things, in the order you'll meet them in the build.

- **Reeb's own economy fiberglass.** It's a Therma-Tru with a wood edge, and it
  rots in our humidity. We've seen them fail in as little as twelve months
- **Reeb's wood doors.** Same reason
- **On Guard brickmould.** Always Frame Saver instead
- **Hardwood adjustable sill,** which rots eventually, and **value composite.**
  Composite adjustable, always
- **The Therma-Tru multi-point lock.** It fails, and the 400 Series patio door
  module explains why: Andersen builds theirs in house and Therma-Tru ships to
  distributors who assemble
- **Reeb's sill pan.** Wildly overpriced, and we source locally

## Pricing

Go to Actions, then pricing template, then **homeowner pricing.** Leave price
adjustment alone.

The lock symbol reveals cost, list, price, and margin. **Don't have that on
screen in front of a customer.**

**This price doesn't include labor.** Labor comes in as adders once you import
to Vendo.

## Editing

The description and the blue text on the side are all hyperlinks back into that
part of the build. Some changes force you back through later questions, some do
not.

## Adding more doors

Hit Add and work through it again. Everything saves under one quote number.

**Note the quote ID,** because you need it to import into Vendo.

## Not in the quoting system

If a customer wants something from the catalog that Reeb 2G won't build, you
can submit to find out about pricing and availability. That's a separate
process and not something you resolve at the table.

modules.title: Quoting a custom door in Reeb 2G
modules.body_md:
## Why this comes up more than you would think

**Therma-Tru has close to 5,000 door options in their catalog.** Reeb 2G only
carries part of that, mostly the popular configurations and the things they
keep in stock.

So when a customer picks something you can't find, it usually isn't that the
door doesn't exist. It's that the quoting software doesn't cover it. That
needs a special order.

## Timing

It comes back in **24 to 48 hours**, usually toward the faster end. Longer if Reeb
has to check with their own suppliers on pricing or availability.

You can't price it at the table. You can tell the customer exactly when they'll hear back, which is a much better answer than "let me look into it."

## Submitting

Log in and start a new quote. You'll see the same screen as always, exterior doors,
interior doors, and so on. Scroll down to **Special Order.**

It's an order by description, so what you get is a free text box. You can drag the
corner to make it bigger.

## Write it like they can't see what you're picturing

**This is the whole job.** Reeb doesn't like leaving anything open to
interpretation, and **if you don't include something, they won't include
it.**

A complete description looks like this:

> Therma-Tru Fiber Classic, FCM60 standard six panel solid, 3.0 by 6.8, 1 inch
> cut down, standard 2-3/8" double bore, strike jamb prep, bronze composite
> adjustable sill, ORB hinges, 7-1/2 inch Frame Saver jambs, right hand in
> swing, bronze weather stripping.

Note what that includes: the line, the model, the size, every modification, every
finish, and the handing. ORB is fine, they know it means oil rubbed bronze.

Custom jamb depths are one of the things special order can do. The 7-1/2 inch
in that example would be for an unusual masonry opening, and it's exactly the
kind of thing Reeb 2G won't build on its own.

Anything obvious that's missing comes back as an email asking for it, which
restarts the clock.

## The editing trap

Once you've saved the description, the text becomes a hyperlink. **Clicking
that hyperlink to edit will erase everything you typed.**

**Cut and paste your description somewhere safe before you click into it.**
Then paste it back and make your edits. Annoying, but that's how it behaves.

## Sending it

You need a PO number and a job name before you can submit. Fill those in and check
the marker to save. The [PO naming](module:REF-080) sheet has the convention.

**Project Actions**, then **Send for Special Order Review**, then Send, then
Yes.

The quote locks. You can't touch it while Reeb is working on it, and an
eyeball icon shows they have it. You get an email when it comes back.

## When it comes back

Go to Projects, top right. Your quote will be there with a list price on it.

Click the hyperlink and you get two options: **No, let me edit further**, or
**Yes, I accept.**

**Before you accept, compare the two sides.** The left is what you sent. The
right is what they came back with.

This is the part that matters. Read every line. They can add things, drop
things, or misinterpret something you thought was obvious. It has taken several
resubmittals on occasion, and sometimes you have to get on the phone with them.

If something is unclear, ask. You can reach out to Reeb yourself, or go through
the COO. Whatever we order needs to be unambiguous.

If you need changes, choose edit further and type them in the same kind of box.

## Pricing it

Accepting doesn't price it for the customer. **You still have to apply the
homeowner pricing template**, the same as any other Reeb quote.

In the video the cost was $1,078 and the list came back at $2,157, so the homeowner
price lands where it should.

Then it's ready to order.

modules.title: Quoting Vinyl Design on the iPad
modules.body_md:
Vinyl Design is our vinyl window option, quoted in their own portal rather than in
Vendo. Keep the login on your iPad home screen.

## The Vinyl Design portal

The home screen shows company quotes, not just yours. Orders at the top are
placed orders or special quotes. Company Quotes below shows the ten most recent
across everyone. Search is in the hamburger menu if you need an older one.

Create Quote is where you start a new one.

## Setting up

**Customer is always Window Works Company.** Ignore everything else on the
list.

Under Quote, you only need the **PO number and customer reference number**, and the
[PO naming](module:REF-080) sheet has the convention. Nothing else on that screen
matters.

Under Sales, your name should be populated. **Gross profit margin is manual and
doesn't prepopulate. For in-home sales it is 50 percent, always.** We don't
go below it. Discounts and promotions come later in Vendo.

Hit Add and you have a live quote with a number.

## What we sell

Vinyl Design sells trim coil, roofing, and plenty else. **We sell only their
window line.**

**Mountain View series, almost exclusively.** If a customer insists on meeting
Energy Star, you have to go to Ultra View, their newest line. For practical
purposes it's a Mountain View with tweaks to hit the new values, and it costs
more. Mountain View is already a very energy efficient window, so you aren't
selling anyone short.

## The insert deduction

For an insert into an existing wood frame:

**5/8 inch off the width. 1/2 inch off the height.**

A 28 by 54 opening becomes 27-5/8" by 53-1/2". Fractions or decimals both work.

## Building a window

Quantity defaults to 1. Ignore call size and thickness, because neither is
relevant to us.

**Line item comment is worth using.** Put the room in. It prints on the label
stuck to each window, which helps the project manager and installers find where
things go without a tape measure.

**Construction type defaults to Replacement and that's almost always right.**
New construction comes with a nailing flange and different options. **Ignore
Configured in Sunroom Designer entirely.**

Finish size means exactly what you entered, tip to tip.

**Blue white is a bright white, not blue.** People do ask. Cream white is the
close match to Andersen white, which matters if a house is mixing brands. Cream
white with black laminate is a black exterior.

**No exterior painting.** We don't offer it and it isn't a good product.

**Custom meeting rail** is none.

**Glass** is double pane, double strength, always, with argon rather than krypton.
Standard Low-E comes out of the box and is already efficient, with upgrade adders
available.

**Triple pane** is very expensive for minimal gain in this market. Competitors
push it. Quote it if they insist, but try to talk them out of it.

**Tempered** where code requires it, which the
[Tempered glass and code](module:REF-050) sheet covers.

Obscure or reeded glass for bathrooms, an upcharge, and worth offering where
there's a picture window near a tub.

**Grilles are vertical by horizontal, which is backwards from Andersen.** 2V 1H
is a six over six. Contour or flat, colonial or prairie. Two tone grille colors
if the exterior is dark.

**Half screen with the Better View extruded option, always.** The fiberglass
screen saves a couple of dollars and isn't well made.

**Locks** default to single or double based on width. Flip locks are an upgrade
worth mentioning for children's rooms, because the window locks automatically when
it closes.

**Insulated frame** is a small upcharge for a little more efficiency, worth
offering. **Foam wrap is automatic** and gives you the airtight fit.

**Head expander and sill expander must be added or they don't ship.** The sill
expander in particular is what finishes the outside properly.

## New construction differences

Extension jambs become relevant here. Their poplar is raw and unfinished, it runs
50 to 75 dollars a window, and it isn't a good product. **Better to have our crew
apply them,** or let a contractor buy their own wood. Quote theirs if a customer
pushes for it.

**Nailing fin: leave it unchecked, always.** It acts as flashing and is proper
for installation. It can be cut off in the field if needed, but it can't be
added back.

J-channel is for vinyl siding. It can be removed in the field easily, but not
added, so think about whether it's needed.

## Twin and mulled units

The flow is slightly different. Enter the overall width and height of the whole
unit, then factory mull, then work through the rest as normal.

## Finishing

Surcharge should always be zero, and tax is prepopulated at 7.25 percent for Wake
County.

**For the customer, print Quote Without Pricing.** That gives them all the
specifications, quantities, sizes, and the schematics on the back page, with no
prices. That's what you send. The full priced version is internal.

modules.title: Understanding project adders in Vendo
modules.body_md:
Adders do two jobs. They configure pricing, and they capture the labor for
installation.

Getting them right is how we charge fairly. We don't want to overcharge, and
we also don't want to give labor away.

This module is the walkthrough. The
[Adder traps](module:PR-048) sheet comes next and catalogues the ones that go
wrong, so read that once you've been through this.

## The margin alignment factor

**This one is a tool, not a step.** It's the first adder to go in if you're using
it, and it's your call whether you do.

You'll find it under Configure, then Project Adders, then Select Existing, then
the Service Fees tab. Check the box and it's applied.

It raises the price by 11.11 percent, which gives you room to take discounts back
off during the price conversation.

**Use it when you want discounts to be visible.** A customer who came in through
a popup offering 20 percent off wants to watch 20 percent come off, and a customer
who likes to haggle wants to see you move. The factor is what lets you do that
without touching the margin, because adding 11.11 percent and then taking 10
percent off lands you back where you started.

**Skip it when you'd rather lead with the lowest number.** Some customers just
want the real price first time. You can still apply the three day deal and the
cash discount without the factor in.

Either way, the limit is the same. Past 20 percent total, Vendo requires
authorization and texts leadership.

## Where adders live

**Andersen windows and Andersen patio doors:** inside each line item. Build the
window, then the Adders tab.

**Therma-Tru through Reeb, ProVia, Vinyl Design, DSA:** project level, at the
end.

## Carpentry adders

The things the crew charges us for, so we charge for them.

- **Blinds.** Taking them down and rehanging them
- **Interior shutters.** Usually plantation, and they cost more than exterior
  because they're more work
- **Exterior shutters.** Usually plastic, and easier
- **Brickmould and sill nose replacement**
- **Cutting a window out of an opening.** Comes up with bricked over openings,
  nailing flanges, and old aluminum. Far more labor than it sounds
- **Extension jambs**, field cut and applied
- **Siding repair and rot**
- **Storm window removal.** Rarer now, but it still happens

## Install type drives the price

Replacement, full frame, and new construction each carry completely different
labor and material. The [Install types](module:REF-010) sheet covers the
differences, including the two cases people get wrong.

New construction is significantly cheaper and should only be selected when it
genuinely applies. In-home sales rarely sees it. The professional side does.

## United Inches

United Inches is just the width plus the height of the unit, in inches.

**It isn't a Vendo field.** It's how we band the labor ourselves, because a
bigger, heavier window is more work and more money to the subcontractors who
install it. So you work out the United Inches and that tells you which adder tier
to pick.

Three tiers:

- **102 or less**
- **103 to 125**
- **Over 125**

Worked through on real sizes. A 36 by 60 double hung, which is about as standard
as they come, is 96 United Inches, so it sits in the bottom tier. Go up to a 48
by 72 and you're at 120, which is the middle tier. A 72 by 60 picture window is
132 and lands in the top one.

So two windows that look similar on a plan can fall either side of a tier line,
and the jump is worth checking rather than assuming.

## Doors

Andersen patio doors work like the windows, adders inside the line item.

**Non-Andersen doors** is the tab for ProVia, Therma-Tru, and DSA. Door with a
transom, single, double, triple, single with two sidelights. **A transom is a
separate standalone price.** Miss it and the transom labor is unbilled.

**Big doors can't be quoted in the field at all.** Too much involved, and all
custom. It's a special quote, so you can't give a price on site.

## Vinyl windows

Vinyl Design and ProVia both fall under full frame vinyl or replacement vinyl.

**Full frame vinyl is a rule, not a judgment,** and the
[Install types](module:REF-010) sheet covers why. The short version is that all
vinyl with J-channel and no wood means full frame vinyl, whatever goes back in.

## Two small things

You can't delete a wrong adder. Go back into Select Existing and unclick it.

Always double check the adder count before you move on. Zero on a window we are
installing means you sold the window and gave away the labor.

modules.title: Adder traps
modules.body_md:
Adders are how we capture labor. Every failure below is silent. Nothing warns
you, the quote still looks finished, and the customer still signs. You find out
when the crew invoices for work nobody charged for.

Read this before you build your first quote.

## Do this first, every time

**Margin alignment factor, before you quote anything.** Project Adders, select
existing, Service Fees tab, check it, done.

It adds 11.11% so you have room to discount back down during the price
conversation. There are safeguards that should stop you dropping below the
floor, but the factor has to be in before you build, not after.

If you know the customer just wants the best number out the door and won't
negotiate, you can skip it. If there's any chance they want to feel like they
won something, put it in.

## Adders live in two different places

**Andersen windows and Andersen patio doors:** the adder is inside each line
item. Edit the window, go to the Adders tab.

**Therma-Tru via Reeb, ProVia, Vinyl Design, DSA:** adders go at the project
level, added at the end under Project Adders.

**Line level** applies to that one unit. **Project level** is one cost for the
whole job regardless of how many openings.

## The five traps

**1. The Andersen zero.** After building an Andersen line item the Adders tab
shows a count. If it reads 0 on a window we're installing, you just sold the
window and gave away the labor. Check the number isn't zero before you move
on.

**2. Copy doesn't copy adders.** Copying a window brings across colors, glass,
hardware, grilles, everything. Not the adders. Every copied unit needs its
adders added. This is the easiest one to miss because the copy looks complete.

**3. Reeb imports at quantity 1.** The import pulls in all your doors, then the
non-Andersen door adder lands at quantity 1 no matter how many doors are on the
quote. Three doors means highlighting the 1, deleting it, and typing 3.

**4. Vinyl Design quantity means two different things.** The package adder,
which is the whole window quote as one line, stays at quantity 1. Charge it at
2 and the customer pays for the windows twice. The installation adder lines
take real counts. Casements and double hungs going into existing frames price
the same, so they collapse onto one line at the combined count. New
construction units are separate lines at their own counts.

**5. Transoms are a separate line.** On the non-Andersen doors tab, a door with
a transom needs both the door adder and the transom adder. A missed transom means the crew's
transom labor goes unbilled.

## Taxable service isn't a habit, it's per source

**Vinyl Design package adder: leave it OFF.** Wake County's 7.25% is already
built into the Vinyl Design quote. Checking taxable service double-taxes the
customer.

**Change order adder: ON.** It's a taxable service.

They differ by system, so a rule learned in one place is wrong about half the
time in another.

## You can't delete a wrong adder

Go back into select existing and unclick it. There's no delete.

## United Inches

Several adders are priced by UI. **United Inches = width + height.** A 50 by 50
window is 100 UI.

Tiers are 102 or less, 103 to 125, and over 125. Bigger and heavier means more
to the subcontractors, so the labor price steps up.

## What carpentry adders cover

These are the things the crew charges us for, so we charge for them:

Taking blinds down and rehanging them. Interior shutters, usually plantation,
which cost more than exterior. Exterior shutters. Brickmould and sill nose
replacement. Cutting windows out of an opening, which comes up with bricked-over
or old aluminum units and is more labor than it sounds. Field-cutting and
applying extension jambs. Siding repair and rot. Storm window removal.

Painting is separate and has to be discussed with the customer during the
quote, because they sign off on it in the labor contract.

**We don't offer staining at all.** If they want stained trim, they arrange that
themselves after we're finished.

options: We don't offer staining, only painting

modules.title: Importing a Reeb quote into Vendo
modules.body_md:
Short one. Reeb and ProVia both built integrations with Vendo, so this is a
proper import rather than a workaround.

## The steps

In Vendo, Configure, then the Reeb tab, then the plus sign.

**It may ask you to log in.** It will log you out eventually, so have your Reeb
credentials with you in the field. Nothing worse than being unable to import in
front of a customer.

Copy the quote ID from Reeb 2G. Paste it into Import Reeb 2G Order. Find.

Your doors pull in.

## It imports pricing, not labor

**This is the part that matters.** The import brings across the door pricing
only. The labor lives on the Vendo side and you have to add it.

Project Adders, plus, Select Existing, **non-Andersen doors** tab. That tab
covers ProVia, Reeb, and DSA, anything not built directly into Vendo the way
Andersen is.

Pick the configuration that matches. Single, double, triple, with transom, with
sidelights.

## Then fix the quantity

**The adder lands at quantity 1 regardless of how many doors are on the
quote.**

Three doors means highlighting the 1, deleting it, and typing 3.

This is one of the four adder traps and it's silent. Nothing warns you.

not, and ProVia has no training at all yet.

modules.title: Importing a Vinyl Design quote into Vendo
modules.body_md:
**Vinyl Design is the exception.** Andersen, ProVia Entry Link, and Reeb 2G all
integrate with Vendo. Vinyl Design does not, so this is a manual workaround.

It isn't pretty but it works, and you need it so the quote carries the
contracts, the installation pricing, adders, discounts, and financing.

## What you need from Vinyl Design

Two things: **the quote number and the total.**

## In Vendo

Flip your screen, Vendo doesn't rotate.

Configure, then Project Adders top right, plus, **Create New.**

**Name** it the PO, following the [PO naming](module:REF-080) sheet.

**Description: the quote number goes first.** Not optional.

Two people downstream depend on it. The project manager going out for the final
measure needs to know which windows they're measuring. The purchasing agent
placing the order needs to be certain they're ordering the right quote and not
another house's windows.

After the number, a rough line count with install types. "2 DH insert, 1
casement insert, 1 DH new construction, 1 twin DH new construction." That is
enough.

**Price** is the Vinyl Design total.

**Quantity stays 1.** This is the whole package as one line. Set it to 2 and
the customer pays for their windows twice.

**Taxable service: OFF.** Vinyl Design already includes Wake County's 7.25
percent. Checking it double taxes the customer.

Save.

## Then the labor

Select Existing, **Vinyl Design installation** tab. Pick the unit types. One
pass brings them all over.

**Then fix the quantities, and this is the subtle part.**

Casements and double hungs going into existing frames price the same, so they
**collapse onto one line at the combined count.** Two DH inserts plus one
casement insert is a single line at quantity 3.

New construction units are **separate lines at their own counts.**

Five windows on the quote becomes three adder lines.

## Quantity means two different things here

The package adder stays at 1 deliberately. The installation adder lines take
real counts. Both facts live in this one process and it's easy to cross them.

## Finishing

Finish, then Quote. Promotions, financing, and deposits are identical to every
other product.

**The Vendo output is ugly for Vinyl Design** because there's no real
integration, so no schematics. Send the customer the no-pricing PDF from Vinyl
Design so they can actually see what they're buying.

modules.title: Completing a change order in Vendo
modules.body_md:
A change order adds work to a job that's already sold. Rot found at measure, a
spouse who wants a second door, trim work the crew flagged.

## The one rule that matters most

**A change order adds work.** It can't change materials and it can't change
the products being installed. If the customer wants a different window than the
one on the signed order, that isn't a change order. Stop and talk to the
office.

## The sequence

Vendo, add a new appointment. Find the customer, they're already in the system
because you quoted them. Additional contact if someone needs to sign who wasn't on the original.

Confirm the address. Start time defaults to the next hour and doesn't matter
as long as it's that day. You can start early.

Save. **A clock icon appears.** That's how you pull information forward.

Click it, choose **change order appointment**, not sales appointment. Pick the
quote, confirm the original sales data carries over.

## Pricing the work

Configured screen, plus in the lower right, **product adders.** Any project
level adders from the original deal show here.

Plus, then **create new.** Name it change order. Write a real description:
"rot and repair of dining room, front elevation windows," not "extra work."

**Price is the crew price plus your markup**, entered as the marked up Window
Works price. Quantity 1.

**Taxable service: no.** Tax applies to products, not labor.

Save, then Finish. The quoting card turns blue.

## Quoting

No promotions, this isn't a sales appointment.

If they financed the original, leave their financing selected. If they paid
cash, click out so it sits blank. **Blank means cash.**

Check pricing details to confirm the new item landed correctly against the
previous deal.

## The form

Proceed. You'll see **decline installation agreement. Ignore it,** it's a
non-required form you'll never use here.

Open the **change order form.** Name and address prefill. You fill **scope of
agreed upon work** and **total price.** Write the scope in real detail. One
page, that's the whole document.

## Signature

On this device right now is fastest. Personal device sends an email link.

Hand them the iPad. Start to review, agree to the electronic signature consent,
which carries the same weight as a fully executed contract. Typed or drawn,
both fine.

If they refuse consent you have a problem. Paper is a last resort and not
ideal. Work through the objection.

They complete, hand it back, you hit proceed.

## Sending

**Only the change order.** Not the Ingage presentation, not the inspection
report. The pre-selected option is already right.

Done, Next, Finish. The email is pre-written and includes their signed
document.

modules.title: Sizing conventions
modules.body_md:
Six different systems. Each one belongs to a different product or process, and
mixing them up produces a window that doesn't fit. Most of these mistakes aren't fixable in the field. They're reorders.

## 1. Sash size

**Andersen 400 Series Tilt Wash and Woodwright.** Also how old wood windows
were measured.

You measure the sash, not the opening. Width across the sash, height from where
the upper sash meets the lower sash down to the bottom.

**The four digits are width then height, each as feet and inches.** So the first
two digits are the width and the last two are the height.

`TW2636` is a Tilt Wash, 2 feet 6 inches by 3 feet 6 inches.
`WDH3442` is a Woodwright, 3 feet 4 inches by 4 feet 2 inches.

The same notation turns up on doors, where `3068` is 3 feet 0 inches by 6 feet 8
inches. What differs between manufacturers is what's being measured, not how the
number is written.

The **unit dimension** is larger than the sash size, because the frame adds
roughly three quarters of an inch. The **rough opening** is larger still,
leaving room for shims and insulation.

On both double hungs, stated height runs from the top of the frame to the very
bottom of the sloped sill, so the interior sits a little higher.

## 2. Nominal

**Vinyl windows, Andersen 100 Series, Andersen 200 Series.**

Different from sash size. This is why the 100 Series works well replacing
existing vinyl from new construction, and why the 200 Series is mostly a new
construction product: its nominal sizing can't be customized.

## 3. United Inches

**Adders only.** Width plus height. Tiers at 102 or less, 103 to 125, and over
125. See the adder traps sheet.

## 4. Vinyl Design insert deductions

Doing an insert into an existing wood frame, deduct from the opening:

- **5/8 inch on the width**
- **1/2 inch on the height**

A 28 by 54 opening becomes 27-5/8" by 53-1/2". Enter as fractions or decimals,
the system takes either.

## 5. Reeb doors: slab versus frame, and jamb depth

Door widths in Reeb refer to the **slab**, not the finished unit. A 28, 30, or
34 is the door panel. You still have to account for the frame.

**Jamb depth can't be changed in the field.** Get it wrong and the door gets
reordered.

- **4-9/16"** for a 2x4 wall. This is 70 to 75% of what you'll see.
- **6-9/16"** for a 2x6 wall.
- **9-1/4"** for very thick walls, cinder block and similar. Rare.

## 6. Andersen undersizes doors

Their stated height is the whole product including the frame. Other door
companies quote the panel and add the frame separately.

So **Andersen's 6'8" is actually 79.5 inches.** The doors in the field are
around 82 inches.

**For a standard 6'8" opening you need Andersen's 6'11", which is 82-3/8".**

This catches people. If you select 6'8" because the existing door is a 6'8",
the door won't fit.

## Which Andersen windows match old wood openings

This isn't consistent within a series, so don't generalize from one product.

**Match traditional wood window sizes, no customizing needed:**
400 Series Tilt Wash, 400 Series Woodwright

**Don't match, expect to customize:**
400 Series casement, 400 Series awning, 400 Series picture windows, most
casements from any manufacturer

Custom sizing exists in eighth-inch increments. On the double hungs it gets
expensive fast and you probably don't need it. On the 100 Series it is
forgiving and cost-effective.

## One more, on the 100 Series

The frame is **3-1/4 inches per side**, so 6-1/2 inches of any unit dimension
is frame in both directions. A 12 by 12 picture window leaves 5-1/2 inches of
glass. The smaller the unit, the worse it looks. Applies to the gliders, single
hung, casement, and picture windows.

modules.title: Never sell, always include
modules.body_md:
Every rule here has a reason. The reason matters more than the rule, because a
customer will push and you need to be able to explain rather than just refuse.

Most of these exist because we got burned once.

## Never sell

### Locks and hardware

**Therma-Tru multi-point lock.** Not available through us. The distributor
model means panel fit varies, and these break down anywhere from six months to
a few years. Doors that can't be secured in the field and need repeated
service. Compare with Andersen, who build in-house and make the best
multi-point in the industry.

**Standard plastic locking keeper on the Andersen 100 Series.** Plastic breaks.
Use the metal slimline. See always include below.

### Doors

**Wood-edge economy fiberglass at Reeb.** Reeb's own economy line is a
Therma-Tru with a wood edge. It rots in our humidity. Seen fail in as little as
12 months. Only composite edge: Classic Craft, Fiber Classic, Smooth Star.

**Hardwood adjustable sill.** Hardwood is more durable than the old wood sills
but still breaks down and rots. Composite adjustable never will. Also skip the
value composite adjustable.

**On Guard.** Always standard Frame Saver.

**Raw wood brickmould.** Frame Saver or PVC only. If the door isn't
pre-finished, PVC. Never primed pine, clear pine, oak, or mahogany all the way
around the outside. Small price difference, and it won't make or break the
deal.

**Reeb sill pans.** Wildly overpriced. We source locally for far less when we
need one.

### Andersen

**Optional lift hardware on the 400 Series Tilt Wash.** Andersen moved a piece
of framing up for energy performance and the lift hardware no longer lines up.
It sits above the glass. They still sell it. We sold expensive bright brass
hand lifts to a customer who chose the window for them, then couldn't fit
them. Fine on the Woodwright.

**Sash kits, any brand.** Antiquated and problematic. Most manufacturers have
dropped them. Andersen still offers an E-Series sash replacement kit. We don't
sell it.

**200 Series Tilt Wash.** New construction only. Can't be used for
replacement.

**Narrowline to Tilt Wash conversion kit.** Hyper specific. Skip it 98 to 99%
of the time.

**Garden and hopper windows.** They appear in the Vendo product list. We don't
sell them.

**Andersen stool.** Expensive and unnecessary. We source locally.

**Andersen arch casing.** We use flex moulding, bought locally.

**Andersen exterior trim.** Nice system when it works, but the spacing doesn't
work in brick openings. We use PVC brickmould. White PVC is close enough to
Andersen white that most people don't paint it.

**Removable interior grilles on any 100 Series window.** Not available.
Simulated divided lite or between the glass only.

**A high-end wood species with paint over it.** Mahogany, cherry, oak, or
maple with a painted finish is money thrown away. Andersen sometimes allows the
combination. If the interior is getting painted, quote pine.

**Third party hardware on an Andersen door.** The multi-point lock is built
into the door and Andersen hardware is what works with it. If a customer
sources their own, we won't install it and we take no responsibility for how
the door operates after that.

**Double bore on an Andersen entry door.** They list it. They don't do it
well, it's problematic, and it's very difficult to modify in the field. A
customer who wants a double bore wants a fiberglass door.

### Glass and vinyl

**Triple pane.** Very expensive, minimal energy gain in the Triangle. Some
competitors push it. If a customer insists you can quote it, but try to talk
them out of it.

**Laminated glass** unless there's a reason. Double strength is strong enough.
Hefty upcharge for no real benefit on an in-home replacement.

**Factory-painted vinyl windows.** We don't offer it. Not a good product.

**Vinyl Design extension jambs.** Raw poplar, unfinished, $50 to $75 per
window, and honestly not well made. Better for our crew to apply them, or for a
contractor to buy their own wood. If a customer pushes, you can quote it.

## Always include, without asking

These are a few dollars each and they prevent headaches. Don't present them as
options.

**Slimline metal hardware on the 100 Series.** Roughly $5 to $10 per window.
Metal instead of plastic.

**Auxiliary foot lock on every Andersen gliding door.** About $30 to $35 on the
400 Series, around $15 on the 100 Series. A real deadbolt shoot bolt, operated
with your foot. Can be drilled for a second position so the door locks while
vented. On a several thousand dollar door it's nothing, and it eliminates the
two-by-four-in-the-track era.

**Sill cover on Reeb doors.** A couple of dollars, protects the sill in
transit.

**Head and sill expanders on Vinyl Design inserts.** If you don't add them
they don't ship. The sill expander in particular is needed to finish the
outside properly.

**Full screen on Andersen windows.** Andersen charges the same for half and
full, so there's no reason to quote a half screen unless the customer asks.
Note that doors are the opposite: they don't default to a screen, and
Andersen's hinged door screen is awkward enough that a phantom screen is the
better answer.

**Unassembled on every Andersen two panel gliding door,** not just the 400
Series. The 100 Series is the only one with no option, and four panel gliders
only come unassembled.

**Knockdown on Andersen gliding doors.** $100 to $200 cheaper, safer to
handle, one person can deliver it, far less damage in transit. Our crews
assemble in 15 to 20 minutes. **The 100 Series is the exception and can't be
ordered knockdown,** because its frame is integrally built.

**Ask about a key lock on every Andersen door.** It's never a default and it
can run over a hundred dollars. Customers assume it's included, and when
nobody asks, we end up ordering it afterward at our own cost.

Now that you know the products, this is where you see them.

We walk the floor together and go through what each display actually is: what's a

customer.

**Including what isn't on display.** Some of what you'll sell isn't on the floor,
and part of this is how you talk about those products without one in front of you.

The product modules deliberately don't tell you what's in the showroom, because
what's on the floor changes. This session is where you find out.

modules.title: Ingage practice
modules.body_md:
Ninety minutes to get comfortable delivering the presentation.

Run it start to finish, out loud, more than once. Spread it over a few days
rather than doing it all in one sitting.

**Out loud matters.** Reading it silently tells you what's on the slides. It
doesn't tell you which slide you have no words for, or where you're reading the
screen instead of talking to the person in front of you.

Hit the completed button when you're ready and we'll set up your test out.

An hour building a real quote in Vendo, using the windows and doors on display in
the showroom.

Champion Sales Rep course.

scenario twice and hearing what you did differently the second time is the point

Hit the completed button when you're done and we'll take a look at your session

Visit an installation site while our crew is working. You'll go with the project
manager, meet one of our install crews, and watch them work.

Take CompanyCam photos while you're there, to the standard covered in the

You run a full appointment end to end, in a real house, the way you would with a
customer. Measure it, build the quote in Vendo from your own numbers, and present
it in Ingage. Then we debrief it.

A real appointment runs about ninety minutes. You have three hours, so there's

We'll confirm your day.

modules.title: Planning your in-store hours
modules.body_md:
Your contract sets eight showroom hours a week, on a schedule we agree with you
and review at the end of training. This is that review.

Come with the hours that work for you and we'll settle your standing weekly
schedule from the week of September 14 onward.

modules.title: What comes next
modules.body_md:
Training ends and the week of September 14 starts, which is your first week
running your own appointments.

Not much changes on paper. You keep your showroom hours, you keep going to the
department meeting, and the reference sheets stay where they are. What changes is
that the appointments are yours.

**We'll ride along on some of them in the first few weeks.** Watching a real
appointment is the only way to give you feedback that's worth anything, and it's
easier to fix something in week one than in month three.

## The first evaluation

Your first evaluation is at 90 days, and the employment contract module covers
how it works. It scores the seven core values, and one of them is Strong Sales.

For a rep, that means four things.

**Closing at or above 30% of the leads assigned to you.** We do our best to
qualify leads before they reach you, though we can't catch every one.

Thirty percent is a starting point rather than the target. Where we want you is
40% and above, and the gap between those two numbers is roughly what the first
year is for.

**Documented follow-up.** Notes and activities in the CRM showing what you did on
the deals that didn't close, not only the ones that did.

**Engagement in department meetings.**

**Using your showroom hours well**, on product education and getting your
questions answered.

Nothing on that list should be a surprise in November. If any of it is off before
then, you'll hear about it before then.

## What to go back to

Most of what you'll need again is in the reference sheets rather than the
modules. They're written to be reread rather than remembered, so go back to them
as often as you want.

- **Install types.** Replacement, full frame, and new construction, and how to
  tell which one you're looking at
- **Adder traps.** The adders that get missed, and what it costs when they are
- **Sizing conventions.** How sizes are written and read, so a quote and a
  measurement mean the same thing
- **Tempered glass and code.** Where code requires it, and where it's a choice
- **Never sell, always include.** The things that have to be on a quote whether
  or not the customer asks

Alright, that's everything. Now get out there and sell some windows and doors.
We know you're going to be great at it.

modules.title: Submitting an initial quality request in Andersen Access
modules.body_md:
How we get Andersen to replace or credit something that arrived wrong.

## The steps

Andersen Access, **My Tools**, second item down, **Initial Quality Requests.**

You can review submitted ones from here. **Start New Request.**

Look up the order by Andersen order number, PO number, or quote number. Select
the specific line item with the problem.

## Choosing a resolution

**Service request** if someone has to go out and change a part.
**Replacement** if we need the part sent.
**Credit** if the customer would rather accept the issue and take money back.

Then the expected date with a reason, any special instructions, and a
replacement PO named as customer plus component. "Frager Sash." Your
information autofills.

Save for Later exists if you need to come back.

## Describing the issue

The terms aren't self explanatory:

**Aesthetic defect.** A ding, a shift, excessive overfill, a cosmetic problem.

**Damage visible.** The box itself was damaged.

**Concealed damage.** The box was fine and you found the damage on opening.

**Photos are required on everything.** Always.

## Then Pipedrive

Submit, and it appears on the pending requests page. Takes a day or two to
populate.

**Update Pipedrive so we can track the order acknowledgement.**

## Two things that aren't software steps

**Check parts before they go to the job site.** The example in the video is an
IQR against an IQR: Andersen sent replacement sashes and one of the
replacements was damaged. It was caught because someone checked before a crew
was standing in a customer's house.

**Filing against a replacement is normal.** Don't assume you've made a
mistake.

modules.title: Quoting big doors and Andersen entry doors in Vendo
modules.body_md:
Advanced tier. Two things we don't sell often, covered together.

Andersen calls the moving glass wall systems **big doors**, which is a fairly
silly marketing name, but it's what they went with. Bifold and multi-glide.

## The three numbers to know before anything else

**$1,700 to $2,300 per linear foot,** depending on how it's built and
configured.

That is **the door only.** No labor, no wall work, no engineering.

A 16 foot opening is tens of thousands of dollars before anyone picks up a
tool.

People see these on HGTV and design shows and have no idea what they cost.
Knowing the range means you can find out in thirty seconds whether this is a
real conversation.

## Why you can't quote it at the table

**No stock sizes.** Everything is custom.

**Minimum 2x6 wall, often more.** If it isn't a new construction opening being
built for it, the wall will probably have to be modified, and that means
engineer reports.

**There are no adders in Vendo for these.** Look and you won't find them. No
standard installation price exists, because it depends entirely on the size and
the project. Labor is a custom quote.

You can build the door in Vendo and give a rough idea of the door cost. You
can't give a price on the spot.

**Hand it to the COO.** They own it from there.

**Realistic timeline: one to two weeks minimum.** An engineer likely has to
come out, the project manager or the installing crew has to see it, and we have
to confirm the build and availability with Andersen. This is nothing like the
24 to 48 hours on a Reeb special order.

## The sales advice that matters most

If you're quoting a whole house and they also want a big door, **quote the
rest of the house and break the big door out into a second appointment or a
second package.**

Close the deal on everything else. Don't let a one to two week engineering
process hold up a house full of windows.

## The economical alternative

Before you deep dive a big door, find out what they actually want.

If they're after that wide open feel, **the 200 Series, 400 Series, or
E-Series four panel gliding doors** get you a very similar look. They customize
up to roughly 16 feet and they're significantly less expensive.

**We never use the word cheap.** More economical, less expensive, better value.
Not cheap.

## The pass-through window, and Andersen doesn't tell you this

If a customer mentions Andersen's **pass-through window**, that's a multi-glide
door or a folding patio door. They're the same product. Andersen just markets
it under a different name and never says so.

You quote it under multi-glide patio door. Because these are fully custom, they
can be made small. A kitchen opening onto a patio for passing food out is a
real use case.

## Building a multi-glide

Traditional or contemporary profile. Most people buying these want light, so
contemporary is the likely pick.

Measurement type is frame size or rough opening. No stock sizes.

Configuration codes read from the exterior. **S3L** is one stationary panel and
three sliding left. There are a lot of combinations.

Glass, grilles, hardware, and locks work like every other Andersen quote.

**Sills, and one of these is a hard rule:**

- **On-floor drainage** is the traditional sill and **the most energy efficient
  and airtight.**
- **Flush** is recessed into the floor for a completely smooth transition.
- **On-floor low threshold** sits between them, less of a trip hazard.

**The flush sill requires a concrete floor.** It can't go into a wood floor.
Andersen's own installation instructions still show wood, but from an
engineering standpoint, after how they have revised it over the last few years,
concrete only. If there's no concrete, it's a traditional sill.

Frame configuration is jamb to jamb, meaning it closes against the wall, or
pocket, where the panels disappear into the wall. That's separate from which
direction they travel.

Panel stack location is whether the stacked panels end up inside or outside.

Power operator automation is available if they want the door motorized.

## Building a bifold

Same flow. Copy your previous choices to move faster.

Configuration codes work the same way. **5L** is five panels folding left. You
can set one panel to swing independently as the everyday door, so they aren't
opening the whole wall to walk outside.

**Minimum 6-9/16" wall depth** on bifolds.

Same sill logic, same concrete rule on flush.

## Andersen entry doors

Different product entirely, and we rarely sell them. Maybe eight to ten in
fifteen years.

Two reasons. They have always been expensive, although compared with what
fiberglass costs now that's less true. And **the options are extremely
limited.** Half light, six panel, a craftsman style, and that's about it.

**Don't bring them up.** You'll sell a fiberglass door almost every time.
Only quote one if a customer is specifically asking for it.

If you do:

**Their residential entry doors use traditional door sizes,** unlike their
patio doors. So a 3'0" by 6'8" is genuinely a 6'8". Ironic, and worth knowing
so you don't apply the undersizing rule here.

Wood inside and out, or aluminum clad.

**Panel thickness: 1-3/4" as standard.** They also offer 2-1/4". Default to
1-3/4" unless someone asks.

**Multi-point lock, always.** They offer a single point but there's no reason
to take it. Andersen's multi-point is a solid product.

**Never sell a double bore Andersen door.** They list it, but they don't do it
well, it's problematic, and it's very hard to modify in the field. If a
customer wants a double bore, that's a fiberglass door.

**Unlike big doors, entry doors do have adders.** Single door installation.
Capture it.
